Before she could move…
Another tall, imposing guy stood before her.
“Not again,” she thought.
He wore dark shades, which immediately set off Violet’s internal alarms.

Wait. Dark shades. Indoors.
Her blood went cold.
She knew those shades.
The audition. The stage. The questions that made her want to disappear.
It was him.
The Alpha who had humiliated her in front of every district.
The one she'd defied.
The one she couldn't stop thinking about, no matter how hard she tried.
Violet’s heart pounded, and a weird tingle ran through her, a warmth settling in her
stomach....
Behind those shades, she felt the weight of his gaze sizing her up, his eyes raked over
her body.
Suddenly, his lips twisted into a wild, unsettling grin.
“Welcome, my purple flower.”
Those words. "Purple flower."
A chill crawled down her spine.
She'd only said her name once, on that stage, under those lights. But he hadn't just
remembered it — he'd twisted it into something intimate. A pet name. Like he'd been rolling it
around in his mind ever since, savoring it, reshaping it into something that belonged to him.
Like he'd already claimed her.
And that meant he hadn't stopped thinking about her since the audition.
Then… high above them… The Luna Board stirred. A new name burned into the stone at
the very bottom of the list.
Number Twenty: Violet Purple.
Whispers and gasps all around.
The new girl… the strange one with purple hair and golden eyes… had already made the
Luna Board on her very first day.

The Alpha’s smile widened. Like he knew something she didn’t.
Violet’s fear spiked.
She ran. She didn’t look back. Not even once.
She tore through the halls of Lunaris at a full sprint.
Students flattened themselves against the walls as she passed.
Her pulse wouldn’t settle.
Her lungs burned.
Left. Right. Down a corridor she didn’t recognize.
She finally skidded to a stop when her legs refused to keep going.
Silence swallowed her.
No wolves. No whispers. No Luna Board.
Just her ragged breathing echoing off the walls.
“Get it together,” she muttered.
This wasn’t District One.
No one here knew how many times she’d been cornered in an alley.
No one here knew what it felt like to go to bed hungry.
To fight for space. To survive.
She’d handled worse than rich wolves with attitude problems.
Roman’s chaos. Griffin’s violence. Asher's obsession.
Three Cardinal Alphas in one day. And every single one of them had touched her life before
she'd even unpacked.
She straightened. “They don’t scare me,” she said under her breath.
A lie. But one she’d lived on before.

Footsteps approached.
“Wow,” a familiar voice said lightly. “You move fast for a new girl.”
Violet turned.
Alice stood at the end of the corridor, arms crossed, slightly breathless.
“You’ve been here ten minutes,” Alice continued, walking closer. “And you’ve already
collided with three Cardinal Alphas and triggered the Luna Board.”
Violet felt that familiar prickle crawl up her spine. “What does that mean?”
“It means,” Alice said carefully, “something is reacting to you.”
The word landed heavy.
Alice hesitated. Then, quieter:
“Principal Jameson is going to want to see you.”
“Why?”
“Because when the Luna Board moves unexpectedly…” Alice’s expression hardened.
“Lunaris notices.”
Violet’s throat went dry. “Great,” she muttered.
Alice leaned in close. "Violet… whatever happens in there, don't let Jameson make you
feel safe. She answers to the Alphas. Everyone here does."
It was the first time Alice's voice had lost its edge.
And that scared Violet more than anything.
Alice gestured down the hall.
“Come on. Before this gets worse.”
As she knocked Principal Jameson's office, a voice called out, "Come in."
She smiled as Violet walked in. "Welcome, Violet." But her smile faltered when she saw the
bruise marks on Viole's neck.
"Who did this to you?" she demanded, her voice full of worry.

For the first time since arriving, Violet felt a flicker of hope. Finally, someone was going to deal
with that jerk. She quickly explained what had happened, describing the red haired guy in detail.
But as she spoke, Principal Jameson's expression changed from anger to something much
worse: fear.
"You mean Griffin Hale did this to you?"
"Griffin Hale? Is that his name?" Violet asked.
"Yes, Miss Purple," Principal Jameson began, her voice suddenly cautious. “And you shouldn’t
be cavorting with him on your first day.”
She exhaled slowly, fingers tightening on the edge of her desk.
“There are… expectations here, Miss Purple.”
Violet frowned. “About what?”
Jameson hesitated.
“About who gets noticed. Who gets protected.”
Violet crossed her arms. “And who doesn’t.”
Jameson didn’t argue.
“Most of that attention is already spoken for,” she said carefully. “Bloodlines. Families. Girls who
were raised for this world.”
Violet looked up.
“There is one student in particular,” Jameson added. “A very special one…”
Viole's stomach tightened. "You're talking about Autumn Carson."
Jameson looked up, surprised. "You've heard the name."
"Hard not to. Everyone here says it like a prayer."
Jameson's voice lowered. "Then you understand what you're walking into."
"What I don't understand is why it involves me."
Jameson exhaled slowly.
"Because something reacted to you."
"Something?"

"One of them," she corrected. "Possibly more than one."
“And I’m guessing that’s not possible.”
Jameson’s expression darkened.
“It shouldn’t be.”
Silence stretched between them.
“If you are compatible with one of the Cardinal Alphas,” Jameson said carefully, “it changes
things.”
“For who?”
“For everyone.”
Violet swallowed.
“And if I’m not?”
Jameson’s eyes flicked briefly toward the window… toward the Academy beyond.
“Then today was a very dangerous coincidence.”
A knock at the door.
Alice poked her head in
“Alice, take Mrs. Purple to the Infirmary,” Jameson said quietly. “Get those marks treated.”
Violet turned to leave.
“Miss Purple.”
She paused.
“If the Luna Board moves again…”
Jameson’s voice dropped.
“Pray it’s only one of them.”
Violet swallowed hard and left with Alice for the infirmary.
As they walked through the gothic Lunaris corridors, Alice reached into her bag and handed
Violet a box.
“That’s your Lunaris welcome pack. Go ahead. Open it.”
Violet hesitated, then unzipped the bag. Textbooks. Supplies. And a sealed phone box.
Her breath caught.
“No way,” Violet whispered, lifting it out.
Alice smiled, all warmth again. “We give devices to scholarship students. Helps you stay
connected. Just log into the Lunaris Academy app. Campus Wi-Fi is everywhere.”
Violet turned the box over in her hands.
“Come on,” Alice said brightly, already moving again. “Let’s get you to the infirmary and have
those wounds checked.”
As Violet followed, phone still in her hand, the words of Principal Jameson wouldn’t leave her: “If
the Luna Board moves again… Pray it’s only one of them.”
Moments later, they entered the grand, impressive infirmary ward.
A healer, one of those super-rare werewolves who could do healing magic, was lecturing a
student… a guy whose arms were covered in fresh burns.
Violet barely registered the actual healer before her attention snapped to the guy.
“You can't keep doing this to yourself, Alaric,” the healer scolded.
"I'm fine," he grumbled, obviously annoyed, as the healer's magic soothed his burns.
Violet couldn’t be sure, but she thought she saw faint sparks crackle across his skin, dancing
like trapped lightning.
And she noticed that no one else stood close enough to touch him.
He must have felt Violet staring because he turned, and their eyes met.
Holy moly. Violet forgot to breathe. Her cheeks turned pink.
He had whitish-blond hair framing a face that was ridiculously good-looking.
But it was his eyes that really got her:

Stormy blue, like a gathering storm.
“That’s Alpha Alaric,” Alice whispered.
Great. Another Alpha. But this one seemed different somehow…
“No one can touch him,” Alice added.
“Why?” Violet asked.
Alice didn’t answer, but cryptically stared at the burn marks on his arms.
Violet studied him.
He had a quiet intensity, but instead of being cocky, there was an innocence about him that was
strangely attractive.
With those striking sapphire eyes, he could have easily been the most handsome alpha she'd
met today…
His gaze swept over her, head to toe, like he was checking her out, sending a surprising jolt
through her.
But just as quickly as that little flicker of excitement appeared, it was squashed by his sudden
cold, dismissive attitude.
His expression made it clear: he wasn't interested.
Any idea that he might have been was shattered by his icy indifference.
"You're good to go," the healer said, finishing up with him.
Done, Alaric brushed past Violet…
And in that quick, fleeting touch, a spark jolted through her.
It was like static shock, sharp, unexpected, and strangely exciting.
Violet froze, her breath catching in her throat…
Alaric stopped short.
He looked down at his hand.
Then at Violet.
Confusion flickered across his face… sharp, startled, unmistakable.

He touched her… and she was fine.
As if his lightning didn’t surge… but recoiled.
Like it had hit something it couldn’t burn through.
His storm didn’t harm Violet. It hesitated.
How?
For a split second, the storm in his eyes surged.
Then his expression slammed shut, colder than before.
Without a word, he turned and walked out.
Violet stood there, heart racing, skin still tingling.
“Did you see that?” Violet whispered.
Alice was staring at Alaric’s retreating back.
“That’s impossible,” Alice said under her breath.
“What is?” Violet demanded. “What just happened?”
Alice looked at her slowly.
“Alaric doesn’t touch people.”
“I noticed.”
“No,” Alice said, shaking her head. “You don’t understand. He can’t.”
Violet frowned.
“Alaric controls lightning. Not metaphorical lightning. Actual voltage. His body discharges
constantly. Static. Current. Storm build-up. That’s why no one stands near him.”
Violet looked down at her own hands.
“But he touched me.”
Alice nodded once.
“And you didn’t burn.”
Violet swallowed.

Silence settled between them.
“Why?” Violet asked.
Alice hesitated.
“The Cardinal Alphas aren’t like other wolves,” she said carefully. “They were born under a lunar
anomaly. People say the Moon Goddess gave them powers.”
She ticked them off quickly.
“Griffin has shockwave strength. He can level stone with a punch.”
“Roman is a Shapeshifter. Any animal. Total chaos.”
“Asher?” She lowered her voice. “Mind manipulation. Thoughts. Memories. Control.”
“And Alaric…” She glanced toward the door. “Storms. Lightning. Energy strong enough to
paralyze a room.”
Violet’s skin tingled again.
“So what does it mean that I’m, like, okay?”
Alice held her gaze.
“It means one of two things. Either you’re resistant to Alpha power… or you’re compatible with
it.”
The word hung between them.
Compatible.
Violet’s throat went dry.
“With him?” she asked quietly.
Alice didn’t answer right away.
“That’s the question,” she said.
Violet wondered what it all meant.
"You,” the healer interrupted. “What can I do for you?" the healer asked, her eyebrows furrowing
as she looked Violet over. "You're new here, aren't you?"
Violet nodded.

" And already in the infirmary on your first day?" The healer shook her head, clucking her
tongue.
"Good luck, kid."
"I know," Violet whispered, her voice barely there. "I know."
“It's nothing serious. You're good to go,” the healer said, handing her some painkillers, and then
Alice took Violet to the dorm rooms.
“Welcome to West House, Violet. This is your home now, and over there are the other houses:
East, South, and North.”
“Whoa!” Violet breathed, staring at the impressive buildings.
“Ms. Purple, you see, this school is all about hierarchy. Human or werewolf, everyone forms
packs in their houses. The four strongest cardinal alphas study here and run these four houses.
Everyone else follows their lead. They are basically gods here.”
Violet sighed. She had already seen the glimpses of student power on her very first day.
Alice continued, “The West House you are going to be in is run by Alpha Asher Nightshade.”
Violet's stomach clenched.
Of course it was.
Of all four houses, she'd been placed in his.
The Alpha who'd humiliated her on stage. The one who'd grinned at her in the hallway like he
owned her. The one who called her "purple flower" like it was already decided.
This wasn't random. It couldn't be.
“Don't worry,” Alice interrupted before Violet could ask. “Anything else? Everything you need to
know is on your phone, plus your roommates will fill you in. Go meet your roommates.”
As Violet entered her room, her roommates looked at her with surprising eyes.
"No way, it's really her," one of them said, sounding shocked.
Violet raised an eyebrow. Why did everyone at this school seem to know who she was?
"Hi, I'm Lily Fairchild," a girl chirped. "It's so nice to meet you, Violet Purple!"
Violet blinked, totally surprised by the sudden friendliness.

"The grumpy one over there is Hazel Sterling," Alice said, pointing to another blonde who
looked permanently scowling.
When their eyes met, Violet immediately felt the dislike radiating from Hazel.
Alice leaned in closer to Violet. "Hazel's just jealous of you."
Violet frowned. "What do you mean she's jealous of me?" she asked Alice, then turned to Hazel.
"No offense, but we literally just met. Why would you be jealous of me? That makes zero
sense."
“Offense taken!” Hazel said.
“Oh, really, Hazel? Seriously? Your ego is out of control, especially after you were just gossiping
about that video,” Lily finally chimed in.
“What video?” Violet asked
All three girls turned to her, looking at her like she was totally clueless.
“You haven't checked your newsfeed,” Lily said.
"Newsfeed?" Violet echoed, even more confused.
“BioDome,” Lily explained. “It's where everyone at Lunaris Academy gets all the school news.
And yeah, you're kinda trending right now.”
Before she could even grab her phone to search for this BioDome thing, Alice had hers out.
Alice searched for the video using Violet's name, and there it was.
Violet's eyes widened as the video started playing.
It was a clip of Griffin manhandling her.
“Oh, God! Who the hell got...”
As she watched herself, awkward and vulnerable, the thought that the entire school had seen
her like that burned in her chest.
“Gods, you’re so lucky,” Hazel sneered from her bed.
“Lucky?!” Violet shook her head, exasperated. ""What are you talking about? What's so special
about these guys that everyone's losing their minds?"
"The Terror Four," Lily answered with a wry smile. “Most of us would kill to even be seen by
them! But unfortunately, only those ranked between first and twentieth have their attention."

Violet’s stomach tightened.
She thought about the green-haired thief.
The red-haired brute.
The one with lightning under his skin.
And Asher…. The obsessive one.
This wasn’t coincidence. This felt like gravity. Forced proximity.
As if her life hadn’t started today by accident, but on schedule.
As if she hadn’t come to Lunaris to learn about the Cardinal Alphas…
But to change them.
“So,” Alice grinned. “Any Alpha you like?”
“What?” Violet blinked.
“You’re in the top twenty now,” Lily said. “They’ll see you as an equal.”
But Hazel scoffed. “Please. They’re all practically taken.”
“Yeah, but no one’s officially Luna yet,” Alice shot back.
Hazel’s smile turned sharp. “Don’t kid yourself. Autumn’s already been raised for that crown.”
Violet stiffened. “Autumn.”
For a split second, her mind traced back to Principal Jameson’s office…
“There is one student in particular,” Jameson had said. “Her name is Autumn.”
Hazel continued. “Number one. Never challenged. And she doesn’t lose.”
Autumn was the girl Lunaris had been preparing for.
The one everyone assumed would be chosen.
The one the rules were built around.
What none of them knew yet…
Was that Violet, the strange purple-haired girl standing in front of them, wasn’t meant to follow
that rule.

She was meant to break it.
For now, Violet's patience finally snapped. "All right, enough! It’s not like I am even interested."
She looked each of them in the eye. "I'm so sick of the ridiculous drama at this school!"
Violet's roommates were speechless. A heavy silence filled the room.
Violet didn't wait for any response. Turning her back to them, she lay down on her bed and
closed her eyes, shutting them out. Sleep came quickly, her body exhausted and her mind still
buzzing from the day's craziness.
That night, Violet’s life changed!
Violet stirred in her sleep. Strong arms wrapped around her. A face buried into her purple hair.
It felt so good she instinctively snuggled closer. His scent was intoxicating. And somehow
familiar…
Then she opened her eyes.
She was back on the stage of the audition. No other girls. No audience. No cameras.
Just her. And Asher.
No. This had to be a dream. He was in her head.
Alice's warning crashed through her mind: He can plant thoughts, erase memories — basically
puppet-master you.
This was his power. And she was trapped inside it.
She broke free from his hold and stumbled back.
"Is this my dream?"
"I might be in your head, but this feels pretty real to me." His voice dropped to a low whisper.
"And it could be real for you, too. If you let me."
Something in Violet's blood reacted… humming, answering him before her mind could stop it.
"Where's my body?" she snapped.
"Your body's in your room. Your mind's here with me."
The scene shimmered. Shifted.
When Violet blinked, she was straddling Asher on a bed in a room she'd never seen before.
Black stone walls. Candlelight. The air thick with incense.
His world. His rules.
She tried to move, but she couldn’t.
"Calm down, baby," he murmured.
Violet's skin crawled. She was disgusted by him. But her body wouldn't cooperate.
That pull was back. Stronger. Insistent.
As if her blood recognized him… even as her mind rebelled.
He looked at her with that dark, hungry gaze. Like he wanted to swallow her whole. Like he'd
been waiting for her forever.
"Be mine, my purple flower," he said. "Be my queen. Rule with me."
"Let me go!" she spat.
"You're the only one who can talk to me like that and get away with it," Asher said. "Do you
know how rare that is?"
"If you want to kill me, just do it. I'm not begging."
"Why would I kill my queen?"
Why was he so obsessed with her? What was it about her that he couldn't resist?
It was the same question she'd had on that stage. The same look in his eyes when she'd
refused his Command. Like she was something impossible. Something he had to have.
"I'm done here," Violet snarled. "Send me back. Now."
"Sure thing," Asher replied smoothly. "But first, I need a little something to remember you by."
Scissors—then, a soft snip echoed in the silence.
A lock of her purple hair rested in his palm.
"You!" Violet exploded.

And just like at the audition — when his Command had tried to break her and failed —
something inside Violet surged.
Not anger. Not fear.
Power.
The dream cracked. The candlelight flickered wild. Asher's grin faltered for the first time.
"What are you—"
She didn't let him finish. She tore herself out of his world like ripping through a wall.
Violet woke with a gasp.
Sweat soaked her sheets. Her heart was racing like she’d been running for her life.
For a second, she thought it had all been a dream.
Asher.
His hands. His voice in her head.
She stumbled into the bathroom, gripping the sink, staring at her reflection.
Her clothes were untouched. Her body unharmed.
Relief hit her…
Then her hand went to her hair.
A chunk was missing.
Violet froze.
Her fingers traced the jagged edge where purple strands should have been.
Her stomach dropped.
It wasn’t a dream.
Asher Nightshade had been inside her head.
And he’d taken something with him.
“I need to get out of this place,” she whispered.

That thought hardened instantly.
Lunaris Academy was a trap.
And she decided right then and there…
She wasn’t going to stay long enough to find out what else it could take from her.
Morning came too fast.
Alice burst into the room like nothing had happened, all cheer and chatter, while Violet dressed
in silence.
The Lunaris Academy uniform fit perfectly. Too perfectly. Like it had been made for her.
Alice noticed the tension immediately.
The way Violet’s shoulders stayed tight. The way her eyes never quite settled, always alert.
Her smile softened.
Alice stepped closer, fixing Violet’s tie for her, hands steady… deliberate.
Protective.
“Listen, Violet,” Alice said quietly. “Power is the only currency here. If you want to be left alone,
you need it.”
Violet didn’t answer.
She didn’t want power. She wanted out.
Alice held her gaze a moment longer than necessary.
As if making a silent promise.
Because Alice knew something Violet didn’t yet… She knew the secret.
The power she was talking about wasn’t something to be gained, or fight for.
Violet already had it.
The dining hall was split in two. Downstairs for the regular students. Upstairs for the elites.
Four oversized thrones sat empty at the center of the upper platform.

Violet didn't need to ask who those belonged to.
After last night's dream — Asher's hands, his voice, the missing lock of hair — she was relieved
those seats were empty.
Then the knot in her stomach tightened. If she was in the top twenty… did that mean she had to
sit up there? With them?
"Earth to Violet!" Alice snapped her fingers. "The line's moving."
A girl waltzed past the entire line and started piling food onto a plate like she owned the place.
Nobody said a word.
"That's Hope," Alice whispered. "Autumn's personal assistant."
Hope carried the tray upstairs and set it down in front of a girl with striking silver hair.
Autumn Carson.
As if she felt Violet staring, Autumn turned and locked eyes with her. The gaze felt like a
challenge.
Violet didn't look away… until she felt Alice grab her arm.
"You're number twenty. Your spot's upstairs."
"I'll eat down here," Violet said, already walking toward a lower table.
The second she sat, the entire floor went silent.
Then Alice's panicked cry — "Violet, look out!"
Violet dodged just in time. Her breakfast crashed to the floor.
A girl stood over her, pure disgust twisting her features. "So this is who they replaced me with?"
Paige. The previous number twenty. The girl whose spot Violet had taken on the Lunaboard
without even trying.
"She's sitting downstairs! She doesn't even know the rules!"
Phones came out. The cafeteria was watching.
Violet calmly brushed crumbs off her clothes and turned her back.
"Hey! I'm talking to you!" Paige shrieked. "Don't ignore me, you daughter of a whore."
That stopped Violet cold.

That word. The same word the girls at the audition had used. The same word that had followed
her mother's name her entire life.
Something inside Violet snapped.
She turned. The storm in her eyes made Paige's smirk falter.
Paige swung. Violet caught her arm and twisted it behind her back.
Violet forced her to face the crowd.
"Listen up. I don't care who you are or what privileges you have at this school. Leave me alone,
and we're good."
Her voice hardened. "And that word — 'whore' — don't ever use it around me."
"You're nothing but a whore, bitch," Paige spat.
Violet dragged her to the spilled food and shoved her face into the mess.
"Where I come from, we don't waste food," Violet said. "If it falls on the floor, you pick it up."
She let go. Paige sobbed into the wreckage.
Silence.
Then, from the elite section, slow clapping.
It spread. The whole cafeteria joined in.
But Violet felt no triumph. Only dread.
This wasn't applause. It was acceptance. Like this school kept testing her — and she kept
passing tests she never signed up for.
Everyone clapped.
Except Autumn. She stared daggers at Violet.
And Violet realized something: every moment since that audition stage had been pulling her
deeper. The acceptance letter. The Luna Board. The dream. And now this.

She wasn't climbing a ladder. She was being dragged toward something.
But what was it? Why was she really here? What was all this leading to?!
She bolted.
She had to find Principal Jameson and drop out of this nightmare. Today.
She ran straight for the administrative floor.
Straight for Principal Jameson.
She didn’t slow down.
Didn’t hesitate.
This was ending now.
She knocked.
No answer.
She knocked again, wondering if Principal Jameson was even there.
Frustrated, Violet turned to leave, then clearly heard, "Come in."
Her heart raced.
This was it.
She'd walk in, demand they revoke her scholarship, and Principal Jameson would do it.
Violet had made up her mind.
She walked in, heart pounding.
She saw Principal Jameson sitting in her executive chair, back turned.
For a second, Violet thought something looked different, like her build was bigger, but she
shrugged it off, figuring it was just her imagination.
Who else would be in the principal's chair?
Ignoring the weird feeling, Violet straightened up.
She cleared her throat, gathering her courage....

“Principal Jameson, I need to talk to you.”
Principal Jameson didn't answer for over a minute.
An awkward silence hung in the air.
Figuring she might as well just come out with it, Violet dropped the bomb.
"I don't want to go to school here anymore, Principal Jameson. Please revoke my scholarship
and give it to someone else."
There, it was out.
Violet felt lighter, like a weight had been lifted.
Now, there was no way the principal could ignore her.
The chair started to swivel.
Violet held her breath, but when the chair finally turned around, the face she saw made her
blood run cold.
You have got to be kidding me!
It wasn't Principal Jameson, it was Asher freaking Nightshade sitting in her chair.
Asher stood, studying her.
“Tell me something, Violet. How did you do it?”
He took a slow step toward her.
“Last night…” His eyes darkened. “You pulled yourself out of my dream.”
He stopped in front of her.
“That has never happened,” Asher said quietly. “The only person who’s ever refused me. The
only person powerful enough to resist a Cardinal Alpha… is supposedly a human with purple
hair?”
Violet’s stomach dropped.
“That means you aren’t what you think you are. You’re not just some whore’s daughter, are
you?”
Her jaw tightened.
“I don’t know where I came from,” Violet said sharply.

Asher smiled, slow and dangerous.
“That’s what makes this interesting.”
“Makes what interesting?” Violet asked, panic rising in her chest.
Asher began circling her. “One of us is supposed to marry Autumn. A real, honest-to-Gods she-
wolf. So that we can breed pureblood Alpha heirs.”
The air between them tightened as he got closer.
“Autumn Carson has spent her whole life believing destiny belonged to her… just because she’s
pureblood,” he said. “But the moment you resisted my command, that destiny changed.”
A faint smile curved his mouth. Another step.
“And once the other Cardinal Alphas realize what you are… they won’t let you go.”
Violet froze as Asher leaned even closer… Close enough to kiss.
“So I need to claim you before they do…”
Violet should have panicked. But once again she was seized by that same strange feeling, torn
between fear and something primal.
“You, my purple queen,” he whispered, “are here to take Autumn’s place.”
Asher wants Violet to take Autumn's place. But Autumn has never lost… how far will she
go to protect what's hers?
Four Cardinal Alphas. Four divine powers. And not one of them could break Violet. So
what happens when they all want her?
Something ancient is hiding in Violet’s blood. Something that terrifies the most powerful
wolves alive. What is she?

She signed the divorce papers while he was asleep.
No argument. No confrontation. She left them on the nightstand, picked up her suitcase, and walked out of the only life she'd ever wanted — because she'd finally understood something she couldn't unknow.
Victor Tillman had never chosen her. Not once in three years.
What Sophia didn't tell him — what she couldn't tell him — was that she was already carrying his children.
Six years later, she has built something real. A research institute. A home. Twin boys named Jayden and Jaymie who are sharp, fearless, and fiercely protective of her in ways that make her heart ache and swell at the same time. She has survived. She has healed. She has almost convinced herself the past is gone.
Then she enrolls her sons in kindergarten — and their new classmate is a quiet little girl named Cassandra.
Victor Tillman's daughter.
The children bond instantly. Naturally. Like pieces that were always meant to fit together. And Sophia watches it happen with cold dread, because she knows what Victor doesn't: those three children share the same father.
She knows what's coming. She just doesn't know how fast.
Victor has never stopped looking for her. When he walks into a restaurant and his daughter is already safe — his first question, the only question that matters to him — isn't about Cassandra at all. It's about Sophia. Where is she? And that single question changes everything, because it tells her exactly how much danger she's in.
What follows isn't a slow unraveling. It's a collision.
His fiancée, Laura, figures out the threat before Victor does. She blacklists Sophia's entire research institute from every supplier in the city. She wages a quiet, vicious war on the woman she sees as competition — threatening not just Sophia's career but the medical research she's spent six years building from nothing. Victor, watching from a distance through a private investigator, is consumed by a jealousy he won't name over a woman he claims to be over.
And three six-year-olds, brilliant and determined, begin maneuvering the adults around them like chess pieces — because they already know what the adults refuse to admit.
They're family.
The breaking point comes not from a confrontation or a revelation or a dramatic accusation. It comes from a feverish little girl reaching out from her father's arms toward a woman she's only known for weeks — and whispering one word.
Mommy.
Everything Victor thought he understood about his life cracks open in that moment. The woman he told to leave. The wife he dismissed for someone else. The family he shattered before he even knew it existed. All of it standing in front of him, impossible to deny.
And the worst part — the part that will haunt him through every episode that follows — is that the more he sees, the more he realizes the damage was his. The separation. The loneliness. The six years his children spent apart from each other and from him. He didn't just lose Sophia.
He broke something irreplaceable.
Mama's Lil Kings is a story about what happens after the worst decision of your life catches up with you. About a woman who chose survival over bitterness and built something extraordinary — and a man who has to decide if extraordinary things can still be rebuilt from ruin. About children who love each other with a certainty their parents haven't earned yet. About secrets that grow for six years and still aren't finished.
100 episodes. Every one of them earns the next.
If you've been looking for a drama that doesn't ask you to be patient — that pays off in every single episode — this is it.

His phone. The little radio he plays in the shower. Kelsey's old clock radio going off in the spare room.

Anything at all except the true thing.

I set the chicken down on the bottom stair. I've thought about that a hundred times since. Some part of me knew I was about to need both hands.

I went up one stair at a time.

The bedroom door was wide open. They hadn't even bothered to close it.

And there she was.

I'm not going to pretend she wasn't beautiful. She was gorgeous. She looked like she'd walked off a magazine cover. Long dark hair down to the middle of her back. Legs up to her neck. Skin like she'd never been awake at 3am a day in her life.

She had nothing on but a black lace bra and my jeans.

She was trying to get the top button through the stiff new denim, and it wouldn't go.

So Gary walked over and did it for her.

He did it the exact way he's done the clasp of my necklace before every wedding and every funeral for 33 years. Thumbs careful. Chin tucked down. Breathing through his nose.

That small, patient thing he used to do for me.

That's what did the damage.

I didn't scream. I didn't cry.

I went downstairs and picked the chicken up off the bottom stair.

A minute later she came down behind me with her purse on her shoulder.

She stepped right past me in my own kitchen like I was a coat rack.

At the door she stopped.

"They're a little loose on me, actually," she said. Soft. Patient. Like she was doing me a favor.

"You can have them back when you get there."

And she walked out to her car wearing my goal jeans.

I opened the refrigerator and put the chicken away.

Right next to the little white box of pens in the door.

My shot pens. They live in the door of my refrigerator, between the creamer and the pickles.

I closed the fridge. I wiped the counter that didn't need wiping.

Then I got in my car and drove.

No direction. I ended up in the Sonic on Route 9 in a town where nobody knows me. I parked in a stall and didn't order a thing. I sat there watching the girls on roller skates carry trays.

I flipped down the visor mirror.

The woman in it was gray. Puffy under the eyes. A face that looked like it hadn't slept in a year, because it hadn't.

I didn't recognize her.

I want you to hear me on something before I go any further.

There is no excuse for what Gary did. He doesn't get forgiven at the end of this.

But by the time that girl got to my closet, there wasn't much of my marriage left for her to take.

It had been leaking out of our house for months. A little more every evening, on my couch, at 7 o'clock.

And it started with a little pen in my refrigerator door.

A pen my doctor was thrilled about.

I know how that sounds. Stay with me anyway.

Because if you're on one of these shots, or you love somebody who is, you're about to recognize your own evenings in this.

I need to tell you who I used to be. Because it matters.

I was up at 5:40 every morning for 22 years.

I knew 600 kids by name. When a first grader threw up in the hallway, I was the one with the mop and the clean shirt from the lost and found before his teacher even looked up.

Every Thursday after dismissal, I walked two miles around the track with the teachers. I started that group. It was mine.

And every Fourth of July, I fed Gary's whole crew in our backyard. Forty people. A brisket I started at 4 in the morning.

That was me.

Then last October, my doctor started me on a GLP-1.

My A1C had been creeping up for three years. I was 205 pounds. Dr. Okafor is a careful man, and kind, and he didn't scare me.

He said, "Terri, at this point food changes alone rarely get people where they need to be. I'd like to start you on a weekly injection."

So I did. And I did it perfectly, because that's how I do everything.

Shot every Sunday night at 8. Pens in the fridge door. Every bite logged in the app. Around 1,100 calories most days. Protein at every meal, like the nurse told me.

And it worked.

Down 11 pounds in the first seven weeks.

At my next visit my A1C was the best it had been in ten years. Dr. Okafor wrote "Great job!" on the printout in blue pen. I stuck it on the fridge with a Hillcrest Hawks magnet.

I was his star patient.

Then the scale stopped.

194. Friday after Friday. Five months.

Same shot. Same 1,100 calories. Same logging. 194.

At month six, Dr. Okafor looked at my chart and said, "Let's step you up to the next dose."

He wrote the prescription and handed it to me with a smile.

I sat in my car in his parking lot holding it.

I should have felt hopeful. I felt scared, and I couldn't have told you why.

And something else started happening, so slow I kept explaining it away.

Sunday nights, shot night, I'd go to bed at 10 and be wide awake at 3. Heart going like I'd run up a hill. My watch buzzing at me about my heart rate. Lying there staring at the ceiling fan over nothing.

By 2 in the afternoon there was a fog behind my eyes.

By 7 o'clock I was empty. I'd sit down on the couch "just for a minute" and wake up at 10:30 with the remote on my chest and the TV asking if I was still watching.

Tired, and wired, at the same time. I didn't know a body could do both.

And on bad weeks, the hunger came back.

A drug that's built to shut the food noise off, and I'd be standing in the pantry at 9pm eating saltines out of the sleeve.

Everybody had an explanation for me.

The women in my Facebook group gave me forty different answers. You're eating too much. You're not eating enough. Muscle weighs more than fat.

One woman wrote, "Either something's medically wrong or you're not being honest about what you eat."

I closed the app and cried in the Hillcrest parking lot before I went in to unlock the doors.

Dr. Okafor ran labs. Thyroid, full panel. Everything came back normal.

"Some people plateau," he said. "Stress can play a role. And at your age, menopause can make this harder."

Menopause.

I went through the change at 50. I know exactly what it felt like. The hot flashes, the bad nights, the mood that came and went like weather.

And I came out the other side of that still running the front office. Still walking my two miles. Still up at 5:40.

This was something else.

This was the lights going off in my house one room at a time.

Then one morning a fourth grader came up to the front counter with a late slip. His mom was right behind him.

He looked up at me and said, "Are you the grandma who works here?"

His mom laughed. Then she saw my face and stopped laughing.

I was 56. I went into the supply closet and stood there with the door shut, holding a box of Kleenex, until the bell rang.

I did try one thing on my own. If you're on the shot, I'd bet you've tried it too.

Protein shakes. Everybody on these shots gets told the same thing. Protein, protein, protein.

I bought them by the case at Costco. Chocolate. One every morning in the car on the way to school.

And I'll be fair to them. The trainer at the Y measured me and said I'd held onto my muscle. That's real.

But the scale never moved. And I never once felt different. My nights stayed the same. My 7 o'clock couch stayed the same.

They were doing an honest job on a part of me that was never the problem.

Here's what those months actually took. One piece at a time.

First it took my Thursday walks.

I started telling the teachers I had to stay late for paperwork. From the office window I could watch them going around the track without me.

Nobody asked twice. By March, nobody asked at all.

Then it took my memory.

A mom I've known for six years came in to sign her son out for the dentist. I looked right at him and his name was gone.

I've known that boy since kindergarten. I had to look it up on the computer while his mother stood there watching me do it.

Then it took the Fourth.

I told Gary the grill was broken. He bought a case of burgers at Costco and fed the crew at the shop instead. Nobody said a word to me about it, and that was worse.

Then it took my evenings.

Gary would ask. A drive out to the lake. Ice cream at the Dairy Queen. A movie on the couch with my feet in his lap, the way we used to.

The answer was always the same.

"Not tonight, babe. I'm so tired."

He stopped asking. And here's the part I'm ashamed of.

I was relieved.

And last, it took my marriage.

Gary used to come up behind me at the kitchen sink and press himself against me, and I'd lean back into him without thinking about it. For 33 years.

I started stepping sideways.

He used to reach for me in the dark, his hand sliding up under my nightshirt, and I'd hear myself say the same four words I said more than any other words that whole year.

"I'm just so tired."

I said them so many times they turned into a wall down the middle of our bed.

The last time Gary and I made love, the Christmas tree was still up.

It was May.

When I finally drove home from the Sonic that night, his truck was gone. So was his duffel bag.

There was a note on the counter, on the back of one of his work order slips.

"I think we both know."

That was all.

I didn't call him. I didn't ask where he went.

But three days later I sat down at the kitchen table to pay the bills, and I opened the credit card statement.

Two charges from the same telehealth company. Every month, going back to January.

One prescription shipped to our house.

One shipped to Gary's shop.

Same shot. Same dose. On our joint card.

He'd bought her one of her own.

She went from a size 14 to my size 10s on the same pen I was taking. Down 26 pounds, while I sat at 194 for five months.

I sat at that table and did the math, and the only answer I could come up with was me.

I let myself go. On a shot that was supposed to fix it. While a girl on the exact same shot sailed right past me.

That's what I believed.

I had it wrong. Something was taking me, a little more every week.

And nobody with a diploma on the wall had ever once looked for it.

If you're living this right now, I need to say something to you directly.

I blamed myself for every bit of it. I told myself I'd gotten old and boring. That some women get the miracle and I'm just not one of them.

And I let Gary look at me the way you look at the recliner. Something that's been in the room so long you stop seeing it.

I didn't know yet that it was being done to me. One Sunday night at a time.

It took my daughter, a FaceTime call, and a 74-year-old woman I've still never met to break it open.

Kelsey came by on a Saturday, two weeks after her father left. She had the baby on her hip.

It was 3 in the afternoon. I answered the door in my robe.

She hugged me with one arm. Then she stood back and looked at me the way you'd look at a stranger who reminds you of someone you love.

She sat me down at my own kitchen table and put Mae in my lap.

"Mom," she said. "I know you're upset about Dad. But this isn't about Dad. You've been like this since Christmas."

And I said the thing I'd never said out loud.

"Baby, I've been this tired since my second shot. Your dad leaving just means I quit pretending."

Then I told her all of it. The 3am heart. The 7 o'clock couch. The walks I quit. The boy whose name I lost. Dr. Okafor saying plateau, saying stress, saying menopause.

The 194.

She didn't say anything for a long minute.

Then she said, "Have you talked to Aunt Jo?"

My sister Jo is 59. She started the same shot I did, about a year before me. And she stalled out the exact same way. I remember her at Thanksgiving, sitting in the porch swing with a blanket while everybody else played cornhole.

Then sometime this year, Jo came back.

At Easter she was down on the living room floor with the babies for two hours. Laughing loud. Color in her face. I'd noticed.

I never asked her how. When your own life is coming apart, you don't have room to wonder about anybody else's.

Kelsey didn't wonder. She FaceTimed her right there from my kitchen table and propped the phone against the napkin holder.

Jo took one look at me and her face changed.

"Oh, Terri," she said. "It's the shot, isn't it."

"I'm stalled," I said. "Five months. And I'm so tired I can't see straight."

"Honey, I'm going to save you a year. It's not your age. It's not menopause. And it's not you."

I opened my mouth and she kept going.

"And before you argue with me, it nearly ended me and Dennis too. You just never knew, because I hid it exactly the way you're hiding it right now."

"Then what is it?"

"Your shot is working fine. That's what's wrong."

I almost hung up on my own sister.

"Jo, if you're about to sell me a supplement, I'm hanging up."

She laughed. "Give me ten minutes. If you still think I've lost my mind after ten minutes, hang up and I'll never bring it up again."

I looked at Kelsey. Kelsey looked at me.

"Ten minutes," I said.

"Have you ever heard me talk about Marlene?"

I hadn't.

"Then before I tell you who she is, I'm going to tell you who she isn't. Because I know exactly where your head's about to go.

She has no website. No Instagram. No powder with her face on the label. She has never tried to sell me one single thing.

She's a 74-year-old widow outside of Joplin who answers her own phone."

"Then who is she?"

"She was a hospital dietitian for 31 years. She planned the meal trays for people coming out of surgery. She watched which patients bounced back and which ones never did, and she paid attention to what was on their trays."

That stopped me. Because a dietitian isn't some woman on the internet.

"How do you even know her?"

"A woman at my church wrote her number on a recipe card in pencil and handed it to me after service. That's how Marlene goes around. Woman to woman. She's never advertised a day in her life.

She won't take a dime. I've tried. She tells me to put it in the collection plate."

"So you called her."

"I sat in my car in the Kroger parking lot with my heart pounding like I was doing something wrong, and I called a stranger off a recipe card.

She picked up on the third ring. She let me talk for twenty minutes straight. The stall. The 3am thing. Dennis sleeping in the recliner. She never interrupted me once.

And when I ran out of words, she said, 'You're not lazy, sweetheart, and you're not broken. Open up your food log and I'll show you what's missing.'"

"Terri," Jo said. "Do you log your food?"

"Every bite. Seven months."

"Go get it."

I opened the app on my phone. Seven months of days. Almost every one of them around 1,100 calories, with a little green check mark.

And on the fridge, right over Kelsey's shoulder, the A1C printout with "Great job!" in blue pen.

"Okay," I said. "I'm looking at it."

"Marlene asked me a question here, so now I'm asking you. What does your scale measure?"

"My weight."

"Right. That's all it can tell you. It can't see a thing that's going on inside you. Same with your labs. They tell you what's floating in your blood today.

Now here's what Marlene tells women when the door's closed."

Jo leaned closer to her phone.

"Every time something hard happens, your body spends magnesium to calm itself back down. A fight with Gary. A kid throwing up in your hallway. A bad night. Every hard day spends a little.

When you run low, the calming down never finishes. Your stress stays switched on, all day and all night.

And when your stress stays on, your body thinks something's wrong. So it holds on. To every pound it can.

That's your stall, Terri. That's your 3am. That's why bad weeks send you to the pantry on a drug that's supposed to stop that."

I looked at Mae in my lap. She was chewing on my napkin.

"And it gets worse on its own," Jo said. "Stress burns through magnesium. So you get lower. So your stress stays up. Round and round."

"Then why has nobody ever checked mine?"

"Hold onto that one. You need to hear the next part first. This is the part where I sat in the Kroger parking lot and cried."

"Marlene asked me what I'd been eating before the shot," Jo said. "And then she asked me what I was eating now.

And she said, 'Honey, almost all of the magnesium your body gets comes from food. What did the shot do to your food?'

It cut it in half.

So it cut your magnesium in half.

That shot is doing exactly what it's built to do. It's turning your appetite way down. It's doing a beautiful job.

And every week it does that beautiful job, you take in less magnesium than the week before. Most women our age were already running low before they ever took a shot."

Something had started to move in my chest.

"Then she asked me three questions," Jo said. "I want you to hear them the way she asked them.

Are you wide awake around 3 in the morning on shot night, with your heart going for no reason?

When you have a bad week, does the hunger come back like the shot quit working?

And are you completely done by 7 at night, and still can't stay asleep?"

My hand was flat on my chest.

The 3am fan. The saltines. The couch.

My whole year, sitting inside three questions from a stranger in Missouri.

"That's when I cried," Jo said. "She listed my week like she'd been sitting in my kitchen.

And Marlene said, 'Your doctor will call that a side effect. I call it arithmetic. You're eating half the food, so you're getting half the magnesium. Nobody told you to put it back.'"

"And that girl," I said. It came out before I could stop it. "She's on the same shot. She lost 26 pounds."

Jo was quiet for a second.

"Terri. She's 31. No kids. Sleeps nine hours a night. She's got nothing in her life to be scared of. She started that shot with a full tank.

You've been spending yours for 56 years. Raising Kelsey. Running that school. Holding up Gary. You were running low before you ever opened that first pen.

Same shot. You started it on empty."

"You asked why nobody checked," Jo said. "Your doctor checked your blood. That's what a normal panel does.

But almost all your magnesium lives inside your cells. A normal panel doesn't look there. You can be running on empty inside and pass every blood test they've got.

There's a test that looks inside the cells. Hardly anybody orders it. It isn't on the standard sheet.

Nobody's hiding it from you. It just falls through a crack.

And Marlene told me something that put a chill down my back. She said, 'You don't need the test, honey. If you're eating half and putting nothing back, you're running low. The test would only tell you how far.'"

I wrote "inside the cells" on the back of an envelope and underlined it twice.

"Now go to your fridge," Jo said. "And your cabinet. Put everything you've done for your weight on that table."

So I did.

The white box of pens out of the fridge door. The case of chocolate protein shakes from Costco. My step counter. The hormone patch my gynecologist gave me last year.

A whole year of trying, lined up on my kitchen table next to my granddaughter's sippy cup.

"Here's the cruel part," Jo said. "Every one of those works.

The shot turns your appetite down. It really does.

The shakes keep your muscle while you lose. Your trainer was right about that.

The walking burns. The patch helps the hot flashes.

And not one thing on that table puts back what the shot takes out."

I looked at all of it. Every one of them doing their honest little job.

Not one of them anywhere near the thing that was draining me.

"That's not you failing," Jo said. "Marlene says that's just math."

And then I did the last bit of math myself. The part Jo couldn't do for me.

The shot came into my house in October.

The 3am nights started in December.

The couch at 7. The walks I quit. The four words in bed. The wall down the middle of the mattress. All of it, since December.

That girl was never the other woman.

The other woman moved into my refrigerator door in a little white box last October.

Then Gary went and bought her one of her own.

That explains Gary. He still doesn't get a pass from me. Better men than him have sat up nights with tired wives.

But for the first time in a year, I wasn't a woman who'd let herself go.

I was a woman who'd been running on empty, a little lower every Sunday night, while everybody told me I was doing great.

"So what puts it back?" I said.

"Magnesium," Jo said. "The right kind."

I actually laughed at her. "Jo. Magnesium's for leg cramps. Mom took it."

"The kind is everything," she said. "Marlene made me write four things down before she'd give me a name. Let me go find the card."

And while she went to find it, Mae started screaming for her sippy cup, and Kelsey had to go, and I told Jo I'd call her back.

I didn't call her back.

I want you to know what I did that night, because it's the most human thing in this whole story.

I drove to the pharmacy on Route 9 at 8:30 at night and bought the biggest tub of magnesium on the shelf.

$11. "Magnesium 500mg" on the front in big letters.

You'd think the protein shakes would have taught me something.

I took two every morning with my coffee. Right on schedule, the way I do everything.

By night 4 I thought maybe I was sleeping a little better. Maybe.

I told myself it was working.

Three weeks later I stood on the scale on a Friday morning.

1. 

Same as the Friday before. And the Friday before that. My watch said my sleep score hadn't changed one point.

And I'd been in the bathroom every morning by 7 for three weeks straight. I was late opening the front office twice.

I called Jo from the Hillcrest parking lot.

"It doesn't work," I said. And I hated how my voice sounded. "I did it right, Jo. Every morning. Three weeks. Nothing moved."

"Take what?" Jo said. "What did you buy?"

"Magnesium. From the pharmacy."

"Go get it out of your purse. Flip it over. Read me the word right after magnesium."

I dug it out. I turned it over in my hand.

"Oxide."

"Oh, honey."

"Oxide is the cheapest form there is," Jo said. "It's what goes in most of the big tubs on the pharmacy shelf because it costs almost nothing to make.

Your body takes in about 4% of it. The rest goes right through you.

That bathroom every morning? That wasn't it working. That was it leaving.

And whatever you felt on night 4, Marlene has a rule about that. The feeling lies. The Friday scale gets the last word.

And your Friday scale just told you the truth about that tub."

I sat there with that $11 tub in my lap, in a school parking lot, feeling like the biggest fool in Missouri.

"Get a pen," Jo said. "I found the card."

"Number one is the form. It has to say bisglycinate. That's magnesium bonded to glycine. It's the kind that actually gets into your cells, and it even crosses into your brain, which is why it calms you down at night. Up to 90% of it gets used.

Number two is the dose. The full 400 milligrams, printed right on the label. If they hide the number inside some blend, they're hiding it from you for a reason.

Number three, it has to be pharmaceutical grade. And they need to tell you where the mineral comes from.

Number four, every batch gets tested by an outside lab. Every one. Not just the first one they ever made."

I wrote it all down on the back of the A1C printout.

"How do you take it?"

"Two gummies before bed. You chew them, so they break down in your stomach like food. That matters more than it sounds on the shot, because the shot slows your stomach way down. A hard pill can just sit there.

And Terri. Listen to me.

You keep taking your shot. Every Sunday night, same as always. Dr. Okafor runs the shot. You don't touch it. This goes alongside it."

I remember thinking that was a strange thing for my sister to say.

It wasn't strange. It was the most responsible thing anybody had said to me all year.

"And what happened to you?" I said. "Really."

"You saw what happened to me. You watched it all spring and never asked.

The 3am stopped first. Inside a week. I slept through shot night for the first time in a year.

Then the scale started moving again. Slow. A pound or two most weeks. I'm down 34 now, same shot, same dose as when I was stuck.

And Dennis."

She smiled at me through the phone, and I saw her go a little pink.

"Last month we were at the Applebee's for his birthday. I came back from the ladies' room and he watched me walk the whole way across that restaurant.

When I sat down he leaned over and said, 'There's my girl.'

He hasn't kept his hands to himself since."

Jo texted me the name that evening. I didn't order it.

I sat at my kitchen table with my thumb over the link and I almost didn't.

Because I'd drunk a whole case of protein shakes for nothing. Because I'd just flushed three weeks of oxide. Because my husband was in an apartment with a girl wearing my jeans, and I was so tired of hoping.

Hope costs something at 56. Every time it comes up empty, it takes a little piece of you with it.

Before Kelsey went to bed she texted to ask what Aunt Jo said. I told her. The oxide. The bathroom. The four things on the card.

She didn't answer for a long time.

At midnight my phone lit up on the nightstand.

"Do it, Mom."

I'd already called Jo back once more before that. Because I needed somebody to be straight with me.

"Tell me the truth," I said. "What's wrong with it? Everything's got something wrong with it."

Jo didn't even pause.

"They're nothing to look at. Two little gummies that taste like candy, in a plain light blue bag. You'll think it can't possibly be enough.

The first week, they won't do a thing for the scale. You'll just sleep. You'll stand on that scale on Friday and think I lied to you.

But Marlene has turned down every vitamin anybody ever tried to hand her for 31 years. She used to throw supplement reps out of the hospital kitchen by their elbows.

And she buys these with her own money. She mails a bag to her daughter in Tulsa on the first of every month."

That's what got me. A woman who'd thrown reps out by the elbow, licking a stamp for her daughter every month.

I ordered it at 12:04.

It's called SPNutrition.

Before I hit the button, I held the bag up against Jo's card myself, the way she told me to.

Bisglycinate. The full 400mg. Pharmaceutical grade, with a Dutch mineral source they'll name for you. Every batch tested by an outside lab.

Four for four.

And when I looked closer, the company had turned down seven cheaper sources to make it that way. Most companies go looking for cheaper.

They've sold out 12 times in the last year, and the wait when they do is four to six weeks. I bought three bags.

The bag came on a Tuesday.

I didn't take one first. I got the pharmacy tub out of the cabinet and set it on the counter next to the light blue bag, and I turned them both around.

On one side: "Magnesium oxide."

On the other: "Magnesium bisglycinate, 400mg."

You didn't need a dietitian. You didn't even need your reading glasses.

I'd been swallowing the cheapest form on the shelf for three weeks and calling it trying.

I laughed out loud, alone in my kitchen. The first time I'd laughed since that Wednesday.

Then I dropped the tub in the trash and chewed my first two before bed.

Night 1, nothing. I want to be honest about that.

Night 3 was a Sunday. Shot night.

I took my shot at 8, chewed my two gummies at 9:30, and the next thing I knew the alarm was going off at 5:40.

No 3am. No ceiling fan. My watch hadn't buzzed once.

I sat on the edge of the bed and cried a little, and I'm not ashamed of it.

End of the first week, I noticed I wasn't on the couch at 7.

I was on the back porch, deadheading my petunias. At 8:45 at night. I didn't want to sit down.

Week 2, my watch sleep score went up 22 points. And that Friday the scale said 192.

Two pounds. After five months at 194.

I took a picture of the scale. I'm 56 years old and I took a picture of my bathroom scale and sent it to my sister.

Jo sent back a row of crying faces.

Week 3 was the worst week of my life on paper. The divorce papers came. Gary's lawyer wanted the boat.

And for the first time in a year, a terrible week didn't send me to the pantry. I noticed on Thursday night that I hadn't opened it once.

That's when I believed it.

Week 5, Denise, the third grade teacher, cornered me at the copy machine. She grabbed my waist with both hands like she was checking a melon.

"What the hell have you been doing? Did you switch shots?"

"Same shot," I said. "Same dose. Since October."

She didn't believe me.

That same week I walked back out onto the track on a Thursday at 3:30. The teachers stopped in the middle of their stretches. I walked all two miles. Slow. But all two.

Kelsey called on a Sunday and I told her a long story about a kid who'd glued his hand to a library book, every name, every detail, start to finish.

When I got done she was quiet.

"Mom," she said. "You sound like you."

Week 9, I went back to Dr. Okafor.

I was down 17 pounds from 194.

He looked at the scale. He looked at my chart. He looked at me.

"That's a real change, Terri. What's different?"

I told him the truth. I added a magnesium supplement, the bisglycinate kind, two before bed.

He nodded slowly. "Good. Your numbers are trending the right way. Let's leave your dose exactly where it is and recheck you in three months."

The higher-dose prescription he'd written me in the spring is still folded up in my purse.

I never filled it.

Nothing about my medication changed. Same pen. Same dose. Same Sunday night at 8.

The shot had been doing its job the whole time. My body finally had what it needed to stop fighting it.

Eleven months after that Wednesday, my doorbell rang at 9 on a Saturday morning.

It was Gary.

He was standing on my front porch holding a Target bag.

"She left," he said. "Back in September. These were at the apartment. I figured you'd want them back."

My jeans. Folded. Tags off.

And I watched my husband try to work out what he was looking at.

If I'd cut my hair he could have said haircut. If I'd been crying he'd have known what to do with that.

But I was just on. Dressed, coffee in my hand, color in my face, a full day in front of me at 9 in the morning. Down 41 pounds from the day I started the shot.

"You look..." he said. And he couldn't finish it.

So he said the only thing he had.

"What did you do?"

Not I'm sorry. Not I was wrong. What did you do.

He said things after that. He'd been doing a lot of thinking. The apartment was too quiet. He missed home.

"Terri," he said. "Can I come home?"

And here's the part I want every tired woman reading this to hear.

The woman on that couch at 7 o'clock would have said yes.

She'd have said yes because saying yes is easier than carrying a divorce by yourself on an empty tank. You take whatever costs the least when there's nothing left in you.

But the woman standing in that doorway had slept through the night. She'd walked two miles on Thursday. She had evenings that belonged to her again.

"No," I said. "And your truck's blocking my mailbox."

I took the Target bag out of his hand and closed my own front door.

That night I went upstairs to my bedroom.

I stood in front of the same closet mirror she'd stood in front of.

And I put on my jeans.

The button went through on the first try. No lying flat on the bed. No sucking in.

There was room at the waist. I could fit two fingers in it.

I turned sideways, slow, the way she had. I ran my hand down my own stomach.

And I heard her voice in my head as clear as that Wednesday. Soft. Patient.

"You can have them back when you get there."

I looked at the woman in the mirror. I recognized her this time.

"I'm here," I said.

Out loud. To an empty room.

There's a man named Jim now. He's a widower, and I met him at Thursday night line dancing at the VFW in October.

The first time I walked in there in my jeans, he leaned over and said, "Ma'am, you've got the best laugh in this room."

Jim never met the tired woman. He only knows this one.

I gave Denise everything. Marlene's four things. The oxide. Flip it over first.

She's 52, and she'd been on the same shot for six months, stuck the same way I was.

Six weeks later she came into the front office at 7:15 in the morning, shut the door behind her, and pulled up her shirt to show me where her scrubs had gotten loose.

Then she said, "Dale noticed. Twice. In one weekend." And she walked out laughing.

Jo didn't let this take me the way it nearly took her. That's how this goes around. Woman to woman. A recipe card in pencil.

If you're on Ozempic, or Wegovy, or Mounjaro, or Zepbound, or one of the telehealth shots that come in a box in the mail.

If you lost a little at the start and then the scale froze, and it's been weeks or months.

If shot night means 3am and a heart you can feel.

If a bad week sends you back to the pantry on a drug that's supposed to make that impossible.

If you said "I'm just tired" to somebody this week and knew, even as you said it, that it wasn't the whole truth.

If your doctor called you a slow responder and your labs came back normal.

If you tried magnesium from the pharmacy and all it did was send you to the bathroom.

If there's a pair of goal jeans hanging in your closet with the tags still on.

Then hear what I needed somebody to tell me.

The shot is working. You're eating half the food, so you're getting half the magnesium, and nobody told you to put it back.

The tub on the pharmacy shelf was never going to do it.

And you are not a slow responder. You started on empty.

And if it's not you, if it's your mom or your sister or the friend at work who keeps saying she's fine, you get to be the Jo in her story. Send this to her.

Here's where I got mine:

https://spnutrition-us.com/pages/advertorial-magnesium

When the bag comes, flip the back over before you take a thing. If the word after magnesium isn't bisglycinate, it isn't the one.

Two gummies before bed tonight. Chew them.

Keep your shot exactly the way your doctor has you on it. Nothing about your medication changes. That's between you and your doctor.

Night one, you'll probably feel nothing. Give it a week for your sleep. Give it a couple more for the Friday scale.

The feeling lies. The Friday scale gets the last word.

They give you up to 90 days to get your money back if it doesn't work for you. Ask yourself whether your last box of pens came with that.

Every Sunday you're on that shot and not putting it back, you run a little lower.

Somebody is going to fit into those jeans.

Make sure it's you.

Terri, 56

P.P.P.S. If you took pharmacy magnesium and nothing happened, your body didn't fail. Read the back of that tub. If it says oxide, about 4% of it ever got used. That's the whole difference.

P.P.P.P.S. They sold out 12 times last year, and when they do, the wait is four to six weeks. Every batch gets tested by an outside lab, so they can't rush it. I keep three bags in my pantry now. now","cards":[],"body":{"text":"I am going to say something that nobody who owns a cat wants to hear and I don't give a f*k if it upsets you.

Switching to a different brand of pate is not going to save your cat.

Not Fancy Feast. Not Tiki Cat. Not Weruva. Not the $68 case of Hill's prescription your vet just recommended.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I tried ALL of it. Every brand. Every protein. Every texture. For two years. And my cat died anyway. Six years old. Kidney failure. Because I spent two years treating a food problem that was never a food problem.

And the worst part? My other cat started doing the same thing. Same vomiting. Same perfect meat tubes. Same slow decline.
