It's 6:40 on a Friday, and I'm sitting in my car outside a little blue cottage on Crestview Drive with my heart going so hard I can feel it in my teeth.

Doug is supposed to be here at 7.

Let me back up.

My best friend Tammy got divorced three years ago, and she has been living like it's spring break ever since.

Lash extensions. Pickleball four days a week. A red Mini Cooper she named "Alimony." She's on every dating app there is.

"Dating at 56 is a contact sport," she likes to say. "Half of them lie about their height, and the other half lie about their wives."

I used to laugh at that. Because I had Doug.

When Tammy showed me her matches, I'd laugh with her and pour another mimosa. On the drive home, I'd say a little thank-you prayer that I'd never have to do any of that.

I was so grateful for my marriage.At least I thought I was. Then, on a Tuesday in September, she called me at 10:12pm.

"Neecy. Are you sitting down?"

"I'm in bed. What's wrong?"

"I'm on Bumble. Doug just popped up in my matches."

I laughed. "Doug who?"

"YOUR Doug, Denise. Doug, 58. 'Separated. Just looking for someone to talk to.' His picture is from your cruise."

"That's not funny, Tam."

"I'm sending you a screenshot."

She did.

It was the picture from our 2019 cruise to Cozumel. I knew that picture. I was standing right next to him in it, in my blue sundress.

He'd cropped me out. You could still see my hand on his shoulder.

I looked over. Doug was asleep right next to me, on his back, snoring like a leaf blower.
.
I got out of bed and went into the bathroom. I didn't turn on the light at first. I just sat on the edge of the tub with the phone in my hand.

My fingers were shaking so hard I dropped it twice.

When I finally turned on the light, I was sweating. My nightgown was stuck to my back, and my heart was pounding in my ears.

I stood up and looked in the mirror.

The bags under my eyes were dark and puffy. My skin was gray. There were lines around my mouth I didn't remember getting, and my hair was in a claw clip, flat and thin at the part.

It was like every year I'd ever lived came down on me at once, right there under the bathroom light.

I sat back down on the tub and stayed there until 2am.

The next morning, he brought me my coffee. On his way out, he kissed my forehead.
"You look tired, babe," he said, and left.

I made a plan.

First I screenshotted his profile and emailed it to myself. Then I made a folder on my phone and named it "Pot Roast Recipes," because Doug has never once looked at anything with the word "recipe" on it.

Then I made Rachel.

Rachel was 54. Retired dental hygienist. Divorced six years. From Springfield, Missouri, in town for a few weeks helping her sister after knee surgery.

I pulled photos off the internet: a sunset over a lake, a cup of coffee on a porch rail, and a scruffy little mutt I found on a rescue website. I named him Biscuit.

Under "About me," I wrote, "Early riser. Loves the Temptations, breakfast for dinner, and anything with Madea in it. If you can't laugh at yourself, swipe left."

I found his profile at 1:48am, lying in bed next to him while he slept.

I swiped right.

He matched with Rachel at 6:14 the next morning. So at 6:16, with my husband downstairs making my coffee, Rachel texted.

Rachel: Hi

At 6:20, he brought me my coffee.

At 6:31, from the garage, he answered.

Doug: Well good morning. Your dog looks like he's got some opinions.

Rachel: He has opinions about everything.

Doug: A woman with a scruffy dog and a Madea habit. I think I'm in trouble already.

That night I lay next to him in our bed with my phone on silent.

At 10:47, his phone lit up the ceiling. He turned it toward the wall and started typing.
My phone glowed under the sheet.

Doug: Thinking about you, gorgeous. How was your day?

I had to go into the bathroom to answer my own husband.

The first week, he was charming. Funny. Sweeter than he'd been to me in years.
Doug: Good morning, beautiful. Did you swim?

Doug: Saw a sunset paint color at Lowe's. Bought a sample just to think of you.

Doug: You've got me checking my phone like a teenager.

Doug: What are you wearing right now, Rachel?

Rachel: Madea pajamas.

Doug: Lord, I'd pay money to see that.

Rachel: Patience.

He talked about our kids like he was the proudest father in Ohio.

Doug: My daughter's getting married in January. She's a nurse, smart as a whip. My son coaches Little League. Best kid in the world.

He sent pictures. Him on his boat. Him at the grill. Then one night, a mirror selfie at Planet Fitness with his shirt off and his stomach sucked in.

The next week, he sent one in just a towel.

Every single one went into "Pot Roast Recipes."

Day 4.
Rachel: Can I ask you something? You're 58 and you're on here. Are you married?

Doug: Ha. Next question.

Day 6.
Rachel: Seriously. Are you married?

Doug: Would I be on here talking to you if I was?

Rachel: That's not an answer, Doug.

Doug: How's Biscuit?
Day 9.

Rachel: I'm not doing this if there's somebody at home. I'm divorced six years, and I'm not walking into anybody's mess.

Doug: Okay. Fair. I'm separated.

Rachel: Separated how?

Doug: It's over. Has been for a long time. It's just paperwork now, and my lawyer's handling that.

Day 15: "Can I FaceTime you tonight? I want to see that smile."

Rachel: I'm a texter, Doug. Old-fashioned that way.

Day 17: "Just a phone call then. I want to hear you laugh."

Rachel: Good things take time.

Day 19: "Five minutes on the phone. I'm begging, Rachel."

I said no every time. He'd know my voice in one word.

Day 20, at 11:58pm, he was lying next to me while I pretended to sleep. My back was to him, my phone screen turned all the way down.

Rachel: So what happened? You and your wife?

That's when he made the worst list I've ever seen of myself.

Doug: You really want to know?

Rachel: I really do.

Doug: She's not the woman I married. Four years of bad sleep, and it's like it ate her alive.

Doug: She used to be gorgeous. Now she's got these dark bags under her eyes like somebody punched her. Her skin's gone gray. She's 55 and she looks 70.

Doug: Same claw clip every single day. Gray sweatpants. At night it's my old Bengals shirt with a hole in the armpit. Red lipstick used to be her date night thing. I haven't seen it in four years.

Doug: Thirty pounds she's put on. Eats cereal standing up at the counter at midnight because she can't sleep.

Doug: Can't remember anything. Left the stove on twice. Forgot our anniversary dinner reservation. Backed into the mailbox in broad daylight.

Doug: At our grandson's Christmas recital, she fell asleep sitting up. Head back, mouth open. I wanted to crawl under the bleachers.

Doug: Sick all the time. A cold every month. Headaches every afternoon.

Doug: She snaps at me for breathing. Cries at Folgers commercials. One minute she's yelling, the next minute she's sobbing in the laundry room.

Doug: And at night, Lord. Around 2 she wakes up soaked through and kicks the covers onto me. Twenty minutes later she's freezing and rips them back. By 3 the comforter's on the floor, and I'm lying on a wet sheet.

Doug: My sister says it's menopause. She hasn't even had the sense to go to a doctor about it.

Doug: Honestly, Rachel? I can't stand the sight of her anymore. I married a 10 and woke up next to somebody menopause changed.

Doug: I don't love her. Haven't in a long time. My lawyer's working on the papers right now. Soon as my daughter's wedding is done, I'm out.

I was lying right there.

Eighteen inches away. In the Bengals shirt. With the claw clip.

And then my face went hot.

It started in my chest and climbed up my neck. My cheeks burned. Sweat ran down my back and soaked the sheet under me.

I couldn't breathe. I kicked the comforter off, and it landed right on top of him.

Doug groaned and shoved it back toward me without looking up from his phone.
Then he typed.

Doug: She's doing it right now. Soaked. Kicked the covers on me again. 

I got up, went to the bathroom, and ran cold water over my wrists until my hands stopped shaking.

For four years I'd been setting three alarms because I didn't trust myself to hear one. Some days I'd sit in the Kroger parking lot for twenty minutes before I had the energy to go in.

I knew I didn't sleep well. I'd known it for years. I just thought it was mine to carry.

I didn't know my husband was lying next to me every night keeping score.

When I came back, there was one more message.

Doug: I'm glad I have you, Rachel. You're the first thing I've looked forward to in years.

He put his phone on the nightstand, rolled over, and kissed my shoulder.

"Night, babe," he whispered.

Day 22.
Doug: I want to take you away. Anywhere you want. Beach, mountains, Vegas, you name it. I'll take a long weekend off. You deserve to be spoiled.

Rachel: I fly home to Springfield next week. My sister's back on her feet.

Doug: Then I'll fly you back here. Somewhere quiet. Just us. Leave everything to me.

Rachel: Let me think about it.

I let him wait two days.

Rachel: Yes.

Doug: You just made an old man very happy.

That afternoon I called my mom in Sarasota.

"Mom? I miss you. Can I come stay with you for a bit?"

She didn't ask anything. She just said, "Your room's ready."

At dinner I told Doug and the kids I was going to see Grandma for a while.

My daughter put her fork down. "Mom. The wedding."

"I'll be back in plenty of time for the wedding prep," I said. "I promise. Dress fittings, cake tasting, all of it. I wouldn't miss it for anything."

Doug drove me to the airport and hugged me at the curb.

"I'll miss you, babe," he said. "Call me when you land."

Mom picked me up in her Buick. She took one look at me and said, "Honey. When's the last time you slept?"

I fell apart in the parking garage. I told her everything. Tammy. The cruise picture. Rachel. The claw clip. The Bengals shirt. The Christmas recital. The lawyer.

"Oh, baby. Why didn't you ask me? I went through the same thing."

"And your father has been an angel. He never once made me feel small about it. He drove me to the doctor himself. He sat up with me at night and wrote down everything that was happening, so we could figure out what I needed. And we found it."

"That's what a husband is supposed to do, Denise."

I cried so hard I had to wipe my face on her seatbelt.

That night she put me in her guest room.

The bed had this big, heavy comforter in a warm caramel color, covered in raised tufted patterns. It hung almost to the floor on every side.

I sat on the edge, and my fingers started tracing the patterns on their own.

I knew those patterns. Not these exactly, but ones just like them.

When I was seven, I used to lie on Grandma's bed at the farm while the grown-ups talked in the kitchen. Her bedspread was heavy like this, with raised patterns you could follow with your finger like a little road. I'd trace them until I fell asleep, and somebody would carry me to the car.

Mom was watching me from the doorway.

"You remember Grandma's," she said. It wasn't a question.

"I'm doing it right now."

"I looked for one like hers for thirty years," Mom said. "Everything in the stores was thin and slippery. Then I finally found this one. Your grandma slept under hers for 52 years, and your grandpa held her hand on that porch until the day he died."

Then she pointed at the bed.

"Now listen to me. You're sleeping under this every single night you're here. I don't care what Doug says on the phone. You get in this bed, and you stay in it."

"Mom..."

She clicked off the hall light. "Get in."

I pulled it up to my chin. The weight of it settled over me, and my whole body let go.
At 2am I woke up hot, same as every night. I pushed it down to my waist. It stayed right there on my legs instead of ending up on the floor, and I was asleep again before I could think about it.

I opened my eyes at 7:40. Sun on the wall. Coffee smell from the kitchen.
I went into Mom's bathroom and looked in the mirror.

Night 1. The puffiness under my eyes was already down. Not gone, but down. I looked like a woman who'd had a rough week instead of a rough four years.
At breakfast, I asked her. "Mom. What is that thing?"

"It's a comforter from Shayla," she said. "Small company. They make them the old way, about 200 at a time. They sell out, and then you wait weeks for the next batch. Sometimes months."

Doug called every day.

"How's your mom?"

"Good. Her physical therapy's going slow."

"I miss you, babe. The house is quiet."

At 11:20 that night, to Rachel: "Counting the days. When can I fly you in?"
I read it in Mom's guest room, under her comforter. Then I put the phone face down and went to sleep.

Night 2. "Dark bags under her eyes like somebody punched her." Lighter.

Night 3. "Headaches every afternoon." It was 4pm, and I didn't have one.

Doug called that evening. "I tried making your pot roast. Don't ask."

"Did you use the onion soup mix?"

"There's onion soup mix?" He laughed. "When are you coming home, Neecy?"

"Mom's doctor wants me to stay through her next appointment."

At 10:50pm, to Rachel: "Found us a place. Little blue cottage on Crestview Drive. Fireplace, big porch. Tell me you're still coming."

Rachel: I want to. But money's tight since the divorce. A flight's just not in the budget.
Doug: Let me get it. Send me your account info.

I couldn't use my own account. One look at "Denise" and he'd know.

So I called Mom's friend Gloria and asked if I could borrow her bank account for a couple of weeks.

There was a pause. Then she said, "Honey, I've been waiting my whole life for somebody to ask me that."

Rachel: Send it to my friend Gloria's Zelle. She'll get it to me.

Doug didn't ask one single question.

Night 4. He sent $480 for the flight.

By then, I had noticed something.

I was sleeping better.

I still woke up hot, but when I pushed the comforter down, it stayed on my legs instead of ending up on the floor. I could get comfortable again and fall back asleep.
And every morning, I felt a little less exhausted.

I didn't want to go back to the way I'd been sleeping at home.

So I pulled up the Shayla site at Mom's kitchen table. They were running a fall sale, and the batch said 9 left.

I ordered a king in oatmilk at 9:52pm.

By 10:30, it said sold out.
Mom read my confirmation email over my shoulder. "So that's the one you're taking home?"

"That's not just a comforter, Mom," I said. "That's my revenge comforter."

Night 5. "Her skin's gone gray." There was pink in my cheeks.

Doug: Get yourself something pretty for our weekend. On me.
$600.

Night 6. "Eats cereal standing up at midnight." I wasn't awake at midnight anymore.

Doug: Get yourself something nice before I get there. You deserve it.
$350.

Night 7. "Can't remember anything." I did Mom's crossword in pen and went to the grocery store without a list. Doug called. "Neecy, I miss you. When are you coming home?"

"Mom's not ready yet."

Night 8. My revenge comforter came.

Some nights a hot flash still woke me at 2, but I'd push it down to my waist and be back asleep in minutes. It never once ended up on the floor.

Rachel had car trouble that day. Doug sent $900 for the transmission.

Night 9. Biscuit needed surgery. Doug sent $1,200 before I finished typing the word.

Night 10. "My sister says it's menopause." I went to Mom's doctor and finally got real answers.

Rachel was short on rent. Doug sent $1,500 and said, "Don't you ever worry about money again, sweetheart."

That's $5,030 in ten days.

Gloria brought every dollar over in cash, in a church envelope with "BISCUIT" written on the front.

That night I sat on Mom's porch and counted it, and my hands were shaking again.

In 2022, we argued for a whole month over a $300 dishwasher. And he'd just sent a stranger $1,200 for a dog he'd never met.

Night 11. "Same claw clip every single day." With Doug's $350, I got my first real haircut in four years. Long layers, and the gray blended in. The claw clip went in Mom's trash.

Night 12. "Thirty pounds she's put on." My jeans buttoned without lying down on the bed. Mom and I were walking two miles every morning.

"My old Bengals shirt." With his $600, I bought a green wrap dress and a pair of heels. The Bengals shirt went in the trash too.

Doug called. "Babe, it's been almost two weeks. Is something wrong?"

"Everything's fine, Doug."

Night 13. "She's 55 and she looks 70." The girl at the Macy's makeup counter asked if I was shopping for my mother's birthday. I said, "No, honey. That's for me."

"I haven't seen it in four years." I bought a tube of red lipstick. The exact shade.
That night my daughter FaceTimed me about centerpieces.

She stopped in the middle of a sentence. "Mom? What did you do? You look like you did in my high school pictures."

"I'm sleeping, baby."

Night 14. Doug called.

"You sound different, Neecy."

"Different how?"

"I don't know. Happy."

"I'm sleeping."

At 11:45 that night, to Rachel: "Two more days. I can't stop thinking about you. This is the start of something, Rachel. I can feel it."

Night 15. Mom's neighbor Diane, a retired paralegal, helped me with some paperwork. Then she gave me the name of the meanest divorce attorney in Ohio.

The next morning, I looked in Mom's mirror one last time before the airport, for the first time in more than ten years, I felt confident again.

At the gate, the agent checked my ID, looked at it, and looked back at me.
"Ma'am, this says you're 55," she said. "I'd have guessed 45."

I flew home on the ticket my husband bought.
Which brings us back to Crestview Drive, 6:40pm, and me in my car with my heart in my teeth.

At 6:55, I let myself in with the code he'd sent Rachel.

I set an envelope on the kitchen island next to the welcome basket. Then I stood by the window.

At 7:02, I heard his car door. Then I heard him fix his hair in the reflection of the window. I've heard that sound for 34 years.

The door opened.

"Rachel?"

I turned around.

Green dress. Heels. Hair down. Red lipstick.

He stopped in the doorway. 

"Neecy?"

"Hi, Doug."

His face went white. "What... what are you doing here? 

"I'm Rachel."

He just stood there holding a bottle of wine and a bouquet of grocery store roses.

"Springfield, Missouri. Retired dental hygienist. Loves Madea." I tilted my head. 

"Neecy, I can explain..."
"The claw clip. The Bengals shirt. The cereal at midnight. Falling asleep at our grandson's recital." I kept my voice even. "You told a stranger all of that. While I was lying right next to you."

He couldn't look at me.

"'I married a 10 and woke up next to somebody menopause changed.' That one's my favorite."

"Baby, I didn't mean..."

He set the roses down on the counter like they'd burned him.

"You look..." He swallowed. "You look like you did when I met you years ago. "

"I know. You paid for it." I smiled. "The dress was $212. The haircut was $185. The flight home was $480. Biscuit's surgery went great, by the way. Gloria says thank you."

"Who's Gloria?"

"She's in my mother's book club."

He sat down on the barstool like his legs gave out.

"What happened to you?"

"I went to my mother's. And I slept."

"That's it?"

"Fifteen nights in a row. In the world's most comfortable comforter. You should try it."
I picked up the envelope and slid it across the island.

"You said your lawyer was working on papers. Mine works faster."

He opened it. His hands were shaking. Thirty-four years, and I'd never once seen Doug's hands shake.

"I'm divorcing you, Doug. And I'm taking half of everything. Half the house. Half the boat. Half your pension."

"Neecy, please. We can fix this."

"There's a folder on my phone called 'Pot Roast Recipes.' Every message. Every receipt. And a picture of you in a towel that my attorney says I'll never have to show the judge, as long as you sign."

He put his head in his hands.

Then he looked up and said, very quietly, "Whatever you've been sleeping under at your mom's. Where do I get one?"

"It's sold out," I said. "They only make 200 at a time."

Then I walked out to my car in heels.

He called eleven times before I got to the highway.

I let it ring.

The next morning, Gloria called.

"Hold on, baby, I'm putting you on speaker. Your mama's got the whole book club here."

I could hear them all. Eight women and a plate of lemon bars.

"Denise," Gloria said. "Your mama showed us your picture from the airport. We've been passing her phone around for twenty minutes."

"I didn't recognize you," somebody said. "I thought it was your cousin."

"Girl, you look like you're about to go to prom," said another one. 

"I'm finally getting good sleep thanks to Shayla. People are starting to see the value, which is why it never stays in stock for long."

Then they started telling me their own stories, one on top of the other.

"I got mine a year ago," a woman named Pat said. "Thirty-one years of marriage, and Gene and I hadn't slept in the same bed since our youngest went to college. Now he pulls me close every night like we're newlyweds. He told our pastor he got his wife back."

"Mine's been on my bed eight months," said Bev. "I used to be in bed by 7 and still wake up tired. Now I'm playing pickleball four mornings a week. My grandkids can't keep up with me."

"I wake up before my alarm," said Keisha. "Before my ALARM. My boys say I'm way less scary. And I got promoted in June. You can't run a school on three hours of sleep, y'all."

"And I don't need concealer anymore," Gloria said. "My hairdresser asked who did my eyes. I said the comforter did my eyes."

Everybody laughed.

Then a quieter voice came on. "Denise, it's Carol. I don't have one yet."

"Me neither," said somebody else. "That's why we're all on our phones."

I could hear them typing.

"It says sold out," Carol said.

"Mine too. Sold out."

"There's a waitlist. It says the next batch is weeks out."

"Pat, how long did you wait?"

"Seven weeks," Pat said. "They only make about 200 at a time."

"Get on the list right now," Mom said in the background. "And the price goes up in the new year, so don't sit there thinking about it."

"Done," said Carol. "I'm on it."

"Me too."

"Me three. Lord, I hope I get one before Christmas."

Gloria came back on. "Baby, you started a stampede."

Then she hung up.

I pulled into my own driveway at 9:15.

The porch light was off. Doug's truck was still two towns over.

I didn't go into our bedroom. I walked straight past it, down the hall, to the guest room.

I unzipped my suitcase and pulled out my revenge comforter. King, in oatmilk.
I shook it out over the bed and let it fall.

It covered everything. It spilled over all four sides of that bed and kept going, almost to the carpet. You couldn't see the mattress, the box spring, or one inch of the bed frame. The whole bed looked soft and full and finished, like something out of Grandma's farmhouse.

I didn't smooth it. I didn't tuck it. I just climbed under.

The weight of it settled over me, and it felt like I was sleeping on a cloud.

That afternoon I put my name on the waitlist one more time. One for my daughter, for her wedding. I want her to start her marriage under the right one, the way Grandma did.

Tammy called that night.

"Well? Did you do it?"

"Filed Monday."

"Neecy. Half of everything?"

"Half of everything. Plus $5,030 for myself and Biscuit."

She laughed so hard she started coughing.

Then she said, "You look like you're in your 40s, you know that? Tell me what you're doing before I hang up."

"They're called Shayla. I'll send you a link. If this batch is still available, order today. If it's not, please get on the waitlist."

more","cards":[],"body":{"text":"I came home at 1 o'clock on a Wednesday and found a 31-year-old girl getting dressed in my bedroom.

She was wearing my jeans.

The size 10s I bought the week I started my weight loss shot. I hung them on the back of the closet door so they'd be the first thing I saw every morning.

The tags were still on.

They fit her.

She turned sideways in my closet mirror and ran her hand down her own flat stomach, slow, the way you'd smooth a bedsheet.

Then she caught my eyes in the glass.

"You're Terri," she said. "The 194."

That was my weight. To the pound.

The number I'd typed into my phone every Friday morning for five straight months, because it would not move.

My husband had been showing her my weigh-ins.

Gary was standing in the bathroom doorway with a towel around his waist. 59 years old. 33 years married to me.

He didn't say one word.

Neither did I.

I looked for maybe three seconds. Then I walked back down to my own kitchen.

Eleven months later, those jeans came back to me in a Target bag.

What I did with them that night is the reason I'm writing this.

That Wednesday was a teacher in-service day, so the front office at Hillcrest Elementary closed at noon.

I've been the secretary at Hillcrest for 22 years.

I'm the one who knows every kid's name, every allergy, and every parent's excuse for being late.

On the way home I stopped for a rotisserie chicken and the coleslaw Gary likes from the deli counter.

I picked up his Friday lottery ticket while I was there, two days early.

It was nobody's birthday. I just felt like taking care of him.

His truck was in the driveway, which made no sense.

Wednesdays he's out measuring jobs until 6. Gary owns a flooring business. Thirty years on his knees laying other people's floors.

My first thought, I swear to you, was that his back had gone out again.

And I was glad I came home early so I could help him.

That's who I was being, in the exact minute another woman was stepping into my clothes upstairs.

I came in through the garage. There was music playing up there. Something with a slow beat.

My brain started handing me kinder stories.

His phone. The little radio he plays in the shower. Kelsey's old clock radio going off in the spare room.

Anything at all except the true thing.

I set the chicken down on the bottom stair. I've thought about that a hundred times since. Some part of me knew I was about to need both hands.

I went up one stair at a time.

The bedroom door was wide open. They hadn't even bothered to close it.

And there she was.

I'm not going to pretend she wasn't beautiful. She was gorgeous. She looked like she'd walked off a magazine cover. Long dark hair down to the middle of her back. Legs up to her neck. Skin like she'd never been awake at 3am a day in her life.

She had nothing on but a black lace bra and my jeans.

She was trying to get the top button through the stiff new denim, and it wouldn't go.

So Gary walked over and did it for her.

He did it the exact way he's done the clasp of my necklace before every wedding and every funeral for 33 years. Thumbs careful. Chin tucked down. Breathing through his nose.

That small, patient thing he used to do for me.

That's what did the damage.

I didn't scream. I didn't cry.

I went downstairs and picked the chicken up off the bottom stair.

A minute later she came down behind me with her purse on her shoulder.

She stepped right past me in my own kitchen like I was a coat rack.

At the door she stopped.

"They're a little loose on me, actually," she said. Soft. Patient. Like she was doing me a favor.

"You can have them back when you get there."

And she walked out to her car wearing my goal jeans.

I opened the refrigerator and put the chicken away.

Right next to the little white box of pens in the door.

My shot pens. They live in the door of my refrigerator, between the creamer and the pickles.

I closed the fridge. I wiped the counter that didn't need wiping.

Then I got in my car and drove.

No direction. I ended up in the Sonic on Route 9 in a town where nobody knows me. I parked in a stall and didn't order a thing. I sat there watching the girls on roller skates carry trays.

I flipped down the visor mirror.

The woman in it was gray. Puffy under the eyes. A face that looked like it hadn't slept in a year, because it hadn't.

I didn't recognize her.

I want you to hear me on something before I go any further.

There is no excuse for what Gary did. He doesn't get forgiven at the end of this.

But by the time that girl got to my closet, there wasn't much of my marriage left for her to take.

It had been leaking out of our house for months. A little more every evening, on my couch, at 7 o'clock.

And it started with a little pen in my refrigerator door.

A pen my doctor was thrilled about.

I know how that sounds. Stay with me anyway.

Because if you're on one of these shots, or you love somebody who is, you're about to recognize your own evenings in this.

I need to tell you who I used to be. Because it matters.

I was up at 5:40 every morning for 22 years.

I knew 600 kids by name. When a first grader threw up in the hallway, I was the one with the mop and the clean shirt from the lost and found before his teacher even looked up.

Every Thursday after dismissal, I walked two miles around the track with the teachers. I started that group. It was mine.

And every Fourth of July, I fed Gary's whole crew in our backyard. Forty people. A brisket I started at 4 in the morning.

That was me.

Then last October, my doctor started me on a GLP-1.

My A1C had been creeping up for three years. I was 205 pounds. Dr. Okafor is a careful man, and kind, and he didn't scare me.

He said, "Terri, at this point food changes alone rarely get people where they need to be. I'd like to start you on a weekly injection."

So I did. And I did it perfectly, because that's how I do everything.

Shot every Sunday night at 8. Pens in the fridge door. Every bite logged in the app. Around 1,100 calories most days. Protein at every meal, like the nurse told me.

And it worked.

Down 11 pounds in the first seven weeks.

At my next visit my A1C was the best it had been in ten years. Dr. Okafor wrote "Great job!" on the printout in blue pen. I stuck it on the fridge with a Hillcrest Hawks magnet.

I was his star patient.

Then the scale stopped.

194. Friday after Friday. Five months.

Same shot. Same 1,100 calories. Same logging. 194.

At month six, Dr. Okafor looked at my chart and said, "Let's step you up to the next dose."

He wrote the prescription and handed it to me with a smile.

I sat in my car in his parking lot holding it.

I should have felt hopeful. I felt scared, and I couldn't have told you why.

And something else started happening, so slow I kept explaining it away.

Sunday nights, shot night, I'd go to bed at 10 and be wide awake at 3. Heart going like I'd run up a hill. My watch buzzing at me about my heart rate. Lying there staring at the ceiling fan over nothing.

By 2 in the afternoon there was a fog behind my eyes.

By 7 o'clock I was empty. I'd sit down on the couch "just for a minute" and wake up at 10:30 with the remote on my chest and the TV asking if I was still watching.

Tired, and wired, at the same time. I didn't know a body could do both.

And on bad weeks, the hunger came back.

A drug that's built to shut the food noise off, and I'd be standing in the pantry at 9pm eating saltines out of the sleeve.

Everybody had an explanation for me.

The women in my Facebook group gave me forty different answers. You're eating too much. You're not eating enough. Muscle weighs more than fat.

One woman wrote, "Either something's medically wrong or you're not being honest about what you eat."

I closed the app and cried in the Hillcrest parking lot before I went in to unlock the doors.

Dr. Okafor ran labs. Thyroid, full panel. Everything came back normal.

"Some people plateau," he said. "Stress can play a role. And at your age, menopause can make this harder."

Menopause.

I went through the change at 50. I know exactly what it felt like. The hot flashes, the bad nights, the mood that came and went like weather.

And I came out the other side of that still running the front office. Still walking my two miles. Still up at 5:40.

This was something else.

This was the lights going off in my house one room at a time.

Then one morning a fourth grader came up to the front counter with a late slip. His mom was right behind him.

He looked up at me and said, "Are you the grandma who works here?"

His mom laughed. Then she saw my face and stopped laughing.

I was 56. I went into the supply closet and stood there with the door shut, holding a box of Kleenex, until the bell rang.

I did try one thing on my own. If you're on the shot, I'd bet you've tried it too.

Protein shakes. Everybody on these shots gets told the same thing. Protein, protein, protein.

I bought them by the case at Costco. Chocolate. One every morning in the car on the way to school.

And I'll be fair to them. The trainer at the Y measured me and said I'd held onto my muscle. That's real.

But the scale never moved. And I never once felt different. My nights stayed the same. My 7 o'clock couch stayed the same.

They were doing an honest job on a part of me that was never the problem.

Here's what those months actually took. One piece at a time.

First it took my Thursday walks.

I started telling the teachers I had to stay late for paperwork. From the office window I could watch them going around the track without me.

Nobody asked twice. By March, nobody asked at all.

Then it took my memory.

A mom I've known for six years came in to sign her son out for the dentist. I looked right at him and his name was gone.

I've known that boy since kindergarten. I had to look it up on the computer while his mother stood there watching me do it.

Then it took the Fourth.

I told Gary the grill was broken. He bought a case of burgers at Costco and fed the crew at the shop instead. Nobody said a word to me about it, and that was worse.

Then it took my evenings.

Gary would ask. A drive out to the lake. Ice cream at the Dairy Queen. A movie on the couch with my feet in his lap, the way we used to.

The answer was always the same.

"Not tonight, babe. I'm so tired."

He stopped asking. And here's the part I'm ashamed of.

I was relieved.

And last, it took my marriage.

Gary used to come up behind me at the kitchen sink and press himself against me, and I'd lean back into him without thinking about it. For 33 years.

I started stepping sideways.

He used to reach for me in the dark, his hand sliding up under my nightshirt, and I'd hear myself say the same four words I said more than any other words that whole year.

"I'm just so tired."

I said them so many times they turned into a wall down the middle of our bed.

The last time Gary and I made love, the Christmas tree was still up.

It was May.

When I finally drove home from the Sonic that night, his truck was gone. So was his duffel bag.

There was a note on the counter, on the back of one of his work order slips.

"I think we both know."

That was all.

I didn't call him. I didn't ask where he went.

But three days later I sat down at the kitchen table to pay the bills, and I opened the credit card statement.

Two charges from the same telehealth company. Every month, going back to January.

One prescription shipped to our house.

One shipped to Gary's shop.

Same shot. Same dose. On our joint card.

He'd bought her one of her own.

She went from a size 14 to my size 10s on the same pen I was taking. Down 26 pounds, while I sat at 194 for five months.

I sat at that table and did the math, and the only answer I could come up with was me.

I let myself go. On a shot that was supposed to fix it. While a girl on the exact same shot sailed right past me.

That's what I believed.

I had it wrong. Something was taking me, a little more every week.

And nobody with a diploma on the wall had ever once looked for it.

If you're living this right now, I need to say something to you directly.

I blamed myself for every bit of it. I told myself I'd gotten old and boring. That some women get the miracle and I'm just not one of them.

And I let Gary look at me the way you look at the recliner. Something that's been in the room so long you stop seeing it.

I didn't know yet that it was being done to me. One Sunday night at a time.

It took my daughter, a FaceTime call, and a 74-year-old woman I've still never met to break it open.

Kelsey came by on a Saturday, two weeks after her father left. She had the baby on her hip.

It was 3 in the afternoon. I answered the door in my robe.

She hugged me with one arm. Then she stood back and looked at me the way you'd look at a stranger who reminds you of someone you love.

She sat me down at my own kitchen table and put Mae in my lap.

"Mom," she said. "I know you're upset about Dad. But this isn't about Dad. You've been like this since Christmas."

And I said the thing I'd never said out loud.

"Baby, I've been this tired since my second shot. Your dad leaving just means I quit pretending."

Then I told her all of it. The 3am heart. The 7 o'clock couch. The walks I quit. The boy whose name I lost. Dr. Okafor saying plateau, saying stress, saying menopause.

The 194.

She didn't say anything for a long minute.

Then she said, "Have you talked to Aunt Jo?"

My sister Jo is 59. She started the same shot I did, about a year before me. And she stalled out the exact same way. I remember her at Thanksgiving, sitting in the porch swing with a blanket while everybody else played cornhole.

Then sometime this year, Jo came back.

At Easter she was down on the living room floor with the babies for two hours. Laughing loud. Color in her face. I'd noticed.

I never asked her how. When your own life is coming apart, you don't have room to wonder about anybody else's.

Kelsey didn't wonder. She FaceTimed her right there from my kitchen table and propped the phone against the napkin holder.

Jo took one look at me and her face changed.

"Oh, Terri," she said. "It's the shot, isn't it."

"I'm stalled," I said. "Five months. And I'm so tired I can't see straight."

"Honey, I'm going to save you a year. It's not your age. It's not menopause. And it's not you."

I opened my mouth and she kept going.

"And before you argue with me, it nearly ended me and Dennis too. You just never knew, because I hid it exactly the way you're hiding it right now."

"Then what is it?"

"Your shot is working fine. That's what's wrong."

I almost hung up on my own sister.

"Jo, if you're about to sell me a supplement, I'm hanging up."

She laughed. "Give me ten minutes. If you still think I've lost my mind after ten minutes, hang up and I'll never bring it up again."

I looked at Kelsey. Kelsey looked at me.

"Ten minutes," I said.

"Have you ever heard me talk about Marlene?"

I hadn't.

"Then before I tell you who she is, I'm going to tell you who she isn't. Because I know exactly where your head's about to go.

She has no website. No Instagram. No powder with her face on the label. She has never tried to sell me one single thing.

She's a 74-year-old widow outside of Joplin who answers her own phone."

"Then who is she?"

"She was a hospital dietitian for 31 years. She planned the meal trays for people coming out of surgery. She watched which patients bounced back and which ones never did, and she paid attention to what was on their trays."

That stopped me. Because a dietitian isn't some woman on the internet.

"How do you even know her?"

"A woman at my church wrote her number on a recipe card in pencil and handed it to me after service. That's how Marlene goes around. Woman to woman. She's never advertised a day in her life.

She won't take a dime. I've tried. She tells me to put it in the collection plate."

"So you called her."

"I sat in my car in the Kroger parking lot with my heart pounding like I was doing something wrong, and I called a stranger off a recipe card.

She picked up on the third ring. She let me talk for twenty minutes straight. The stall. The 3am thing. Dennis sleeping in the recliner. She never interrupted me once.

And when I ran out of words, she said, 'You're not lazy, sweetheart, and you're not broken. Open up your food log and I'll show you what's missing.'"

"Terri," Jo said. "Do you log your food?"

"Every bite. Seven months."

"Go get it."

I opened the app on my phone. Seven months of days. Almost every one of them around 1,100 calories, with a little green check mark.

And on the fridge, right over Kelsey's shoulder, the A1C printout with "Great job!" in blue pen.

"Okay," I said. "I'm looking at it."

"Marlene asked me a question here, so now I'm asking you. What does your scale measure?"

"My weight."

"Right. That's all it can tell you. It can't see a thing that's going on inside you. Same with your labs. They tell you what's floating in your blood today.

Now here's what Marlene tells women when the door's closed."

Jo leaned closer to her phone.

"Every time something hard happens, your body spends magnesium to calm itself back down. A fight with Gary. A kid throwing up in your hallway. A bad night. Every hard day spends a little.

When you run low, the calming down never finishes. Your stress stays switched on, all day and all night.

And when your stress stays on, your body thinks something's wrong. So it holds on. To every pound it can.

That's your stall, Terri. That's your 3am. That's why bad weeks send you to the pantry on a drug that's supposed to stop that."

I looked at Mae in my lap. She was chewing on my napkin.

"And it gets worse on its own," Jo said. "Stress burns through magnesium. So you get lower. So your stress stays up. Round and round."

"Then why has nobody ever checked mine?"

"Hold onto that one. You need to hear the next part first. This is the part where I sat in the Kroger parking lot and cried."

"Marlene asked me what I'd been eating before the shot," Jo said. "And then she asked me what I was eating now.

And she said, 'Honey, almost all of the magnesium your body gets comes from food. What did the shot do to your food?'

It cut it in half.

So it cut your magnesium in half.

That shot is doing exactly what it's built to do. It's turning your appetite way down. It's doing a beautiful job.

And every week it does that beautiful job, you take in less magnesium than the week before. Most women our age were already running low before they ever took a shot."

Something had started to move in my chest.

"Then she asked me three questions," Jo said. "I want you to hear them the way she asked them.

Are you wide awake around 3 in the morning on shot night, with your heart going for no reason?

When you have a bad week, does the hunger come back like the shot quit working?

And are you completely done by 7 at night, and still can't stay asleep?"

My hand was flat on my chest.

The 3am fan. The saltines. The couch.

My whole year, sitting inside three questions from a stranger in Missouri.

"That's when I cried," Jo said. "She listed my week like she'd been sitting in my kitchen.

And Marlene said, 'Your doctor will call that a side effect. I call it arithmetic. You're eating half the food, so you're getting half the magnesium. Nobody told you to put it back.'"

"And that girl," I said. It came out before I could stop it. "She's on the same shot. She lost 26 pounds."

Jo was quiet for a second.

"Terri. She's 31. No kids. Sleeps nine hours a night. She's got nothing in her life to be scared of. She started that shot with a full tank.

You've been spending yours for 56 years. Raising Kelsey. Running that school. Holding up Gary. You were running low before you ever opened that first pen.

Same shot. You started it on empty."

"You asked why nobody checked," Jo said. "Your doctor checked your blood. That's what a normal panel does.

But almost all your magnesium lives inside your cells. A normal panel doesn't look there. You can be running on empty inside and pass every blood test they've got.

There's a test that looks inside the cells. Hardly anybody orders it. It isn't on the standard sheet.

Nobody's hiding it from you. It just falls through a crack.

And Marlene told me something that put a chill down my back. She said, 'You don't need the test, honey. If you're eating half and putting nothing back, you're running low. The test would only tell you how far.'"

I wrote "inside the cells" on the back of an envelope and underlined it twice.

"Now go to your fridge," Jo said. "And your cabinet. Put everything you've done for your weight on that table."

So I did.

The white box of pens out of the fridge door. The case of chocolate protein shakes from Costco. My step counter. The hormone patch my gynecologist gave me last year.

A whole year of trying, lined up on my kitchen table next to my granddaughter's sippy cup.

"Here's the cruel part," Jo said. "Every one of those works.

The shot turns your appetite down. It really does.

The shakes keep your muscle while you lose. Your trainer was right about that.

The walking burns. The patch helps the hot flashes.

And not one thing on that table puts back what the shot takes out."

I looked at all of it. Every one of them doing their honest little job.

Not one of them anywhere near the thing that was draining me.

"That's not you failing," Jo said. "Marlene says that's just math."

And then I did the last bit of math myself. The part Jo couldn't do for me.

The shot came into my house in October.

The 3am nights started in December.

The couch at 7. The walks I quit. The four words in bed. The wall down the middle of the mattress. All of it, since December.

That girl was never the other woman.

The other woman moved into my refrigerator door in a little white box last October.

Then Gary went and bought her one of her own.

That explains Gary. He still doesn't get a pass from me. Better men than him have sat up nights with tired wives.

But for the first time in a year, I wasn't a woman who'd let herself go.

I was a woman who'd been running on empty, a little lower every Sunday night, while everybody told me I was doing great.

"So what puts it back?" I said.

"Magnesium," Jo said. "The right kind."

I actually laughed at her. "Jo. Magnesium's for leg cramps. Mom took it."

"The kind is everything," she said. "Marlene made me write four things down before she'd give me a name. Let me go find the card."

And while she went to find it, Mae started screaming for her sippy cup, and Kelsey had to go, and I told Jo I'd call her back.

I didn't call her back.

I want you to know what I did that night, because it's the most human thing in this whole story.

I drove to the pharmacy on Route 9 at 8:30 at night and bought the biggest tub of magnesium on the shelf.

$11. "Magnesium 500mg" on the front in big letters.

You'd think the protein shakes would have taught me something.

I took two every morning with my coffee. Right on schedule, the way I do everything.

By night 4 I thought maybe I was sleeping a little better. Maybe.

I told myself it was working.

Three weeks later I stood on the scale on a Friday morning.

1. 

Same as the Friday before. And the Friday before that. My watch said my sleep score hadn't changed one point.

And I'd been in the bathroom every morning by 7 for three weeks straight. I was late opening the front office twice.

I called Jo from the Hillcrest parking lot.

"It doesn't work," I said. And I hated how my voice sounded. "I did it right, Jo. Every morning. Three weeks. Nothing moved."

"Take what?" Jo said. "What did you buy?"

"Magnesium. From the pharmacy."

"Go get it out of your purse. Flip it over. Read me the word right after magnesium."

I dug it out. I turned it over in my hand.

"Oxide."

"Oh, honey."

"Oxide is the cheapest form there is," Jo said. "It's what goes in most of the big tubs on the pharmacy shelf because it costs almost nothing to make.

Your body takes in about 4% of it. The rest goes right through you.

That bathroom every morning? That wasn't it working. That was it leaving.

And whatever you felt on night 4, Marlene has a rule about that. The feeling lies. The Friday scale gets the last word.

And your Friday scale just told you the truth about that tub."

I sat there with that $11 tub in my lap, in a school parking lot, feeling like the biggest fool in Missouri.

"Get a pen," Jo said. "I found the card."

"Number one is the form. It has to say bisglycinate. That's magnesium bonded to glycine. It's the kind that actually gets into your cells, and it even crosses into your brain, which is why it calms you down at night. Up to 90% of it gets used.

Number two is the dose. The full 400 milligrams, printed right on the label. If they hide the number inside some blend, they're hiding it from you for a reason.

Number three, it has to be pharmaceutical grade. And they need to tell you where the mineral comes from.

Number four, every batch gets tested by an outside lab. Every one. Not just the first one they ever made."

I wrote it all down on the back of the A1C printout.

"How do you take it?"

"Two gummies before bed. You chew them, so they break down in your stomach like food. That matters more than it sounds on the shot, because the shot slows your stomach way down. A hard pill can just sit there.

And Terri. Listen to me.

You keep taking your shot. Every Sunday night, same as always. Dr. Okafor runs the shot. You don't touch it. This goes alongside it."

I remember thinking that was a strange thing for my sister to say.

It wasn't strange. It was the most responsible thing anybody had said to me all year.

"And what happened to you?" I said. "Really."

"You saw what happened to me. You watched it all spring and never asked.

The 3am stopped first. Inside a week. I slept through shot night for the first time in a year.

Then the scale started moving again. Slow. A pound or two most weeks. I'm down 34 now, same shot, same dose as when I was stuck.

And Dennis."

She smiled at me through the phone, and I saw her go a little pink.

"Last month we were at the Applebee's for his birthday. I came back from the ladies' room and he watched me walk the whole way across that restaurant.

When I sat down he leaned over and said, 'There's my girl.'

He hasn't kept his hands to himself since."

Jo texted me the name that evening. I didn't order it.

I sat at my kitchen table with my thumb over the link and I almost didn't.

Because I'd drunk a whole case of protein shakes for nothing. Because I'd just flushed three weeks of oxide. Because my husband was in an apartment with a girl wearing my jeans, and I was so tired of hoping.

Hope costs something at 56. Every time it comes up empty, it takes a little piece of you with it.

Before Kelsey went to bed she texted to ask what Aunt Jo said. I told her. The oxide. The bathroom. The four things on the card.

She didn't answer for a long time.

At midnight my phone lit up on the nightstand.

"Do it, Mom."

I'd already called Jo back once more before that. Because I needed somebody to be straight with me.

"Tell me the truth," I said. "What's wrong with it? Everything's got something wrong with it."

Jo didn't even pause.

"They're nothing to look at. Two little gummies that taste like candy, in a plain light blue bag. You'll think it can't possibly be enough.

The first week, they won't do a thing for the scale. You'll just sleep. You'll stand on that scale on Friday and think I lied to you.

But Marlene has turned down every vitamin anybody ever tried to hand her for 31 years. She used to throw supplement reps out of the hospital kitchen by their elbows.

And she buys these with her own money. She mails a bag to her daughter in Tulsa on the first of every month."

That's what got me. A woman who'd thrown reps out by the elbow, licking a stamp for her daughter every month.

I ordered it at 12:04.

It's called SPNutrition.

Before I hit the button, I held the bag up against Jo's card myself, the way she told me to.

Bisglycinate. The full 400mg. Pharmaceutical grade, with a Dutch mineral source they'll name for you. Every batch tested by an outside lab.

Four for four.

And when I looked closer, the company had turned down seven cheaper sources to make it that way. Most companies go looking for cheaper.

They've sold out 12 times in the last year, and the wait when they do is four to six weeks. I bought three bags.

The bag came on a Tuesday.

I didn't take one first. I got the pharmacy tub out of the cabinet and set it on the counter next to the light blue bag, and I turned them both around.

On one side: "Magnesium oxide."

On the other: "Magnesium bisglycinate, 400mg."

You didn't need a dietitian. You didn't even need your reading glasses.

I'd been swallowing the cheapest form on the shelf for three weeks and calling it trying.

I laughed out loud, alone in my kitchen. The first time I'd laughed since that Wednesday.

Then I dropped the tub in the trash and chewed my first two before bed.

Night 1, nothing. I want to be honest about that.

Night 3 was a Sunday. Shot night.

I took my shot at 8, chewed my two gummies at 9:30, and the next thing I knew the alarm was going off at 5:40.

No 3am. No ceiling fan. My watch hadn't buzzed once.

I sat on the edge of the bed and cried a little, and I'm not ashamed of it.

End of the first week, I noticed I wasn't on the couch at 7.

I was on the back porch, deadheading my petunias. At 8:45 at night. I didn't want to sit down.

Week 2, my watch sleep score went up 22 points. And that Friday the scale said 192.

Two pounds. After five months at 194.

I took a picture of the scale. I'm 56 years old and I took a picture of my bathroom scale and sent it to my sister.

Jo sent back a row of crying faces.

Week 3 was the worst week of my life on paper. The divorce papers came. Gary's lawyer wanted the boat.

And for the first time in a year, a terrible week didn't send me to the pantry. I noticed on Thursday night that I hadn't opened it once.

That's when I believed it.

Week 5, Denise, the third grade teacher, cornered me at the copy machine. She grabbed my waist with both hands like she was checking a melon.

"What the hell have you been doing? Did you switch shots?"

"Same shot," I said. "Same dose. Since October."

She didn't believe me.

That same week I walked back out onto the track on a Thursday at 3:30. The teachers stopped in the middle of their stretches. I walked all two miles. Slow. But all two.

Kelsey called on a Sunday and I told her a long story about a kid who'd glued his hand to a library book, every name, every detail, start to finish.

When I got done she was quiet.

"Mom," she said. "You sound like you."

Week 9, I went back to Dr. Okafor.

I was down 17 pounds from 194.

He looked at the scale. He looked at my chart. He looked at me.

"That's a real change, Terri. What's different?"

I told him the truth. I added a magnesium supplement, the bisglycinate kind, two before bed.

He nodded slowly. "Good. Your numbers are trending the right way. Let's leave your dose exactly where it is and recheck you in three months."

The higher-dose prescription he'd written me in the spring is still folded up in my purse.

I never filled it.

Nothing about my medication changed. Same pen. Same dose. Same Sunday night at 8.

The shot had been doing its job the whole time. My body finally had what it needed to stop fighting it.

Eleven months after that Wednesday, my doorbell rang at 9 on a Saturday morning.

It was Gary.

He was standing on my front porch holding a Target bag.

"She left," he said. "Back in September. These were at the apartment. I figured you'd want them back."

My jeans. Folded. Tags off.

And I watched my husband try to work out what he was looking at.

If I'd cut my hair he could have said haircut. If I'd been crying he'd have known what to do with that.

But I was just on. Dressed, coffee in my hand, color in my face, a full day in front of me at 9 in the morning. Down 41 pounds from the day I started the shot.

"You look..." he said. And he couldn't finish it.

So he said the only thing he had.

"What did you do?"

Not I'm sorry. Not I was wrong. What did you do.

He said things after that. He'd been doing a lot of thinking. The apartment was too quiet. He missed home.

"Terri," he said. "Can I come home?"

And here's the part I want every tired woman reading this to hear.

The woman on that couch at 7 o'clock would have said yes.

She'd have said yes because saying yes is easier than carrying a divorce by yourself on an empty tank. You take whatever costs the least when there's nothing left in you.

But the woman standing in that doorway had slept through the night. She'd walked two miles on Thursday. She had evenings that belonged to her again.

"No," I said. "And your truck's blocking my mailbox."

I took the Target bag out of his hand and closed my own front door.

That night I went upstairs to my bedroom.

I stood in front of the same closet mirror she'd stood in front of.

And I put on my jeans.

The button went through on the first try. No lying flat on the bed. No sucking in.

There was room at the waist. I could fit two fingers in it.

I turned sideways, slow, the way she had. I ran my hand down my own stomach.

And I heard her voice in my head as clear as that Wednesday. Soft. Patient.

"You can have them back when you get there."

I looked at the woman in the mirror. I recognized her this time.

"I'm here," I said.

Out loud. To an empty room.

There's a man named Jim now. He's a widower, and I met him at Thursday night line dancing at the VFW in October.

The first time I walked in there in my jeans, he leaned over and said, "Ma'am, you've got the best laugh in this room."

Jim never met the tired woman. He only knows this one.

I gave Denise everything. Marlene's four things. The oxide. Flip it over first.

She's 52, and she'd been on the same shot for six months, stuck the same way I was.

Six weeks later she came into the front office at 7:15 in the morning, shut the door behind her, and pulled up her shirt to show me where her scrubs had gotten loose.

Then she said, "Dale noticed. Twice. In one weekend." And she walked out laughing.

Jo didn't let this take me the way it nearly took her. That's how this goes around. Woman to woman. A recipe card in pencil.
